Please only read the below email: 

Hi Arna, I hope you are doing well.

Further to our discussion, we understand that you currently operating an online store / e-commerce website in Pakistan, through which products are sold to customers using a digitally enabled ordering system similar to an online marketplace model.

We have carried out a preliminary review of the relevant provisions of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001 and the Sales Tax Act, 1990, as amended through the Finance Act, 2025. Based on our initial understanding, your business model may fall within the recently introduced tax framework applicable to digitally ordered goods and services sold through locally operated e-commerce platforms, including websites.

From an income tax perspective, the most important recent development is the introduction of section 6A of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001, which applies to payments received for supply of digitally ordered goods or services delivered from within Pakistan through locally operated online platforms, including websites and online marketplaces. Under the First Schedule, the applicable tax rate is:  

1% where payment is made through digital means or banking channels, and 

2% where payment is collected on Cash on Delivery basis through courier services. 

Importantly, tax falling under section 6A is treated as final tax under section 8 of the Ordinance. Accordingly, where receipts fall within section 6A, such amounts are not again subjected to normal taxation under the regular computation provisions, nor are deductions, losses or tax credits ordinarily available against such final-taxed receipts.

At the same time, the precise application of section 6A depends upon the exact business model. In particular, it is necessary to evaluate whether the website is selling its own goods, facilitating third-party vendors in a marketplace model, or supplying digitally delivered services or digital products. This distinction is important because the nature of the receipts, the person responsible for tax collection, and the overall tax profile may differ depending on the underlying arrangement.

From a collection perspective, the law now places specific responsibility on payment intermediaries and courier services. Where payment is processed through digital means, the payment intermediary is required to collect tax from the gross amount payable to the seller. Likewise, where goods are supplied on Cash on Delivery basis, the courier collecting cash on behalf of the seller is required to collect tax at the applicable rate.

On the sales tax side, the law now expressly recognizes e-commerce as sale or purchase of goods conducted over computer networks through websites, mobile applications or online marketplaces having digital ordering features. In the case of digitally ordered taxable goods supplied from within Pakistan during the course of e-commerce, the Sales Tax Act places the liability to collect and pay tax on the payment intermediary in digital transactions and on the courier in Cash on Delivery transactions, at the rate prescribed in the Eleventh Schedule. Presently, the Eleventh Schedule provides for deduction at 2% of the gross value of supplies in respect of digitally ordered goods from within Pakistan through online marketplace, website or software applications.

In addition to the above, if the business is making taxable supplies of goods, ordinary sales tax implications would also need to be evaluated, including registration, output tax reporting, invoicing, and treatment of input tax, subject always to the exact classification of the products being sold and the operating model adopted by the business.

We have outlined through this email a preliminary overview of the key income tax and sales tax implications that may arise in relation to your proposed online business model. You may kindly review the above and share your feedback or any observations you may have. In addition, we would appreciate if you could kindly clarify whether the professional fee you referred to relates only to ensuring income tax and sales tax compliance, or whether it is intended to also cover accounting and bookkeeping services for the business. 

This clarification will help us properly understand the scope of services expected from our side so that we may share with you a more detailed scope of work along with a formal proposal accordingly. In case any part of the above discussion requires further clarification, please feel free to let us know and we would be pleased to explain the matter in further detail.

Kind regards,

:::writing{variant="email" id="92841" subject="Further discussion on possible sales tax structuring options for the proposed business model"}
Hi Arna,

Further to our earlier email outlining the preliminary income tax and sales tax implications of the proposed e-commerce business model, we have also evaluated the possible sales tax treatment under two different operational structures. For completeness, we have briefly outlined below the two possible options so that the overall impact on tax cost and compliance requirements may be considered before finalizing the business model.

The first option would be to consolidate the procurement and sales activities within the SMC company itself. Under this structure, the SMC company would purchase the oil and other materials directly and carry out the commercial sale of the finished product through the online platform. The bottling, labeling and related processing work may still be performed by the existing sole proprietorship as a toll manufacturing arrangement. In such a case, the sole proprietorship would charge conversion or processing charges to the SMC company, and sales tax at the standard rate of 18% would apply on such processing services.

Under this arrangement, the SMC company would be required to obtain sales tax registration and operate under the normal sales tax regime. The company would be able to claim input tax adjustment on the sales tax charged on purchases of goods as well as on the conversion or processing charges billed by the sole proprietorship. When the finished product is supplied to customers, the SMC company would charge sales tax at the standard rate of 18% on the retail value. In the case of e-commerce transactions, the courier company may deduct tax at the prescribed rate (currently 2%) on Cash on Delivery transactions. Such deduction would be treated as adjustable tax and would be available as a credit against the output tax liability of the SMC company. The remaining sales tax payable, after adjusting input tax and the tax withheld through the courier, would then be discharged through the monthly sales tax return filed by the SMC company.

The second option would be to keep the existing structure broadly unchanged, whereby the sole proprietorship continues to procure the oil, carry out bottling and labeling activities, and operate as the manufacturer or supplier of the finished product. In this scenario, the sole proprietorship would obtain sales tax registration, charge sales tax at the standard rate of 18% on the finished product supplied to the SMC company, and discharge the related sales tax liability through its own sales tax returns.

The SMC company, in this arrangement, would primarily function as an online retailer selling the finished product to end consumers through the website. As discussed earlier, under the e-commerce provisions introduced through section 3(7A) of the Sales Tax Act, 1990, where a supplier operates as a retailer other than a Tier-1 retailer and the tax is collected by the courier or payment intermediary, such tax may operate as the final discharge of sales tax liability and input tax adjustment may not be available. Consequently, the sales tax charged by the sole proprietorship on the supply of finished goods to the SMC company would effectively become part of the cost of the product for the SMC company. The SMC company would recover the applicable 2% tax on Cash on Delivery transactions from customers, which would be collected by the courier and deposited with the government.

One practical advantage of this second option is that the SMC company may not be required to obtain sales tax registration or file monthly sales tax returns, since the sales tax obligations would largely remain with the sole proprietorship. However, the corresponding drawback is that any input tax embedded in the supply chain — including sales tax charged on purchases of oil, packaging material or other inputs — would ultimately become part of the cost of the finished product from the perspective of the SMC company.

In light of the above, it would be advisable to evaluate both options by considering the overall supply chain, particularly the amount of input tax embedded in the procurement of oil and other materials from the local market. If a significant amount of sales tax is being charged in the upstream supply chain, operating under the normal sales tax regime through the SMC company may allow recovery of such input tax through adjustment. Conversely, if the embedded input tax in the supply chain is relatively low, the simplified e-commerce mechanism under the second option may provide a more straightforward compliance approach.

You may wish to review the above alternatives and consider which structure appears more practical and commercially viable for your operations. We would be happy to discuss these options further and assist in structuring the arrangement in the most tax-efficient manner.

Kind regards,
:::

یہ ایک بہت اہم practical سوال ہے، کیونکہ **e-commerce framework** آنے کے بعد اکثر لوگوں کو یہی confusion ہو رہا ہے کہ اگر **courier یا payment intermediary tax collect کر رہا ہے** تو کیا پھر seller کو **sales tax registration** کی ضرورت رہتی ہے یا نہیں۔

آئیے اس کو سیدھے انداز میں evaluate کرتے ہیں۔

### 1. Registration کا بنیادی اصول

**Sales Tax Act, 1990 کے تحت section 14** یہ کہتا ہے کہ ہر وہ شخص جو **taxable supplies of goods** کرتا ہے، اسے **FBR کے ساتھ sales tax registration** لینا ضروری ہے۔  

لہٰذا بنیادی اصول یہ ہے کہ اگر آپ **taxable goods supply کر رہے ہیں** تو registration required ہوگا۔

### 2. E-commerce amendment کے بعد کیا فرق آیا؟

Finance Act 2025 کے بعد **section 3(7A)** introduce کیا گیا جس میں یہ کہا گیا ہے کہ:

اگر  
- seller **cottage industry** ہو یا  
- **retailer other than Tier-1 retailer** ہو  

اور اس کے goods **e-commerce کے ذریعے digitally ordered** ہوں، تو:

- **courier یا payment intermediary tax collect کرے گا**  
- اور وہ tax **final discharge of sales tax liability** سمجھا جائے گا  
- اور **input tax adjustment بھی allow نہیں ہوگا**

یہ ایک طرح کا **simplified final tax mechanism** ہے۔

### 3. اب اصل سوال — کیا registration پھر بھی ضروری ہے؟

عمومی طور پر دو scenarios بنتے ہیں۔

**Scenario 1 — اگر seller regular taxable supplies بھی کرتا ہے**  
مثلاً:  
- online کے علاوہ market میں بھی sale کر رہا ہے  
- wholesalers کو supply کر رہا ہے  

تو پھر **sales tax registration لینا پڑے گا** کیونکہ وہ normal VAT chain میں آ جائے گا۔

**Scenario 2 — اگر seller صرف e-commerce کے ذریعے sale کرتا ہے اور Tier-1 retailer بھی نہیں ہے**  
اس صورت میں practical interpretation یہ بنتی ہے کہ:

- courier / intermediary **2% collect کر رہا ہے**  
- وہ **final discharge** treat ہو رہا ہے  
- seller **input tax claim بھی نہیں کر رہا**

اس scenario میں **registration technically ضروری نہیں بھی ہو سکتی**، کیونکہ seller VAT chain میں operate نہیں کر رہا۔

لیکن یہاں ایک practical advisory point بہت اہم ہے۔

### 4. Practical advisory approach (جو ہم عام طور پر clients کو دیتے ہیں)

اگر business **grow ہونے والا ہے** یا future میں:

- turnover بڑھے گا  
- Tier-1 retailer کی definition میں آ سکتا ہے  
- B2B supplies بھی ہوں گی  

تو **sales tax registration لینا بہتر ہوتا ہے** تاکہ بعد میں compliance issue نہ بنے۔

ورنہ اگر business **چھوٹا e-commerce retail model** ہے اور courier **2% tax collect کر رہا ہے**، تو وہ tax **final discharge** treat ہو سکتا ہے۔

### 5. آپ کے کیس میں (جو structure آپ نے بتایا)

آپ نے جو structure explain کیا ہے:

- oil **brother کی company سے purchase ہوگا**  
- SMC company **online store operate کرے گی**  
- courier **COD collect کرے گا**

تو اس scenario میں strong possibility ہے کہ:

- آپ **retailer other than Tier-1 retailer** treat ہوں گے  
- courier **2% tax collect کرے گا**  
- اور وہ **final discharge of sales tax liability** treat ہوگا۔

لیکن final conclusion دینے کے لیے تین چیزیں confirm کرنا ضروری ہوتی ہیں:

- expected **annual turnover**  
- کیا **online کے علاوہ sales بھی ہوں گی**  
- business **air-conditioned mall / chain store** category میں آتا ہے یا نہیں۔

یہ تین factors ultimately determine کرتے ہیں کہ **registration mandatory ہوگی یا simplified e-commerce regime apply کرے گا**۔

دلچسپ بات یہ ہے کہ پاکستان کا e-commerce tax regime اب آہستہ آہستہ **withholding-based VAT system** کی طرف جا رہا ہے، جہاں courier اور payment gateways **mini-tax collectors** بن رہے ہیں۔ یہی model چین اور کچھ یورپی ممالک میں بھی استعمال ہو رہا ہے تاکہ چھوٹے sellers کو VAT compliance سے بچایا جا سکے۔

:::writing{variant="email" id="68154" subject="Further clarification regarding income tax and sales tax implications for the proposed e-commerce business model"}
Hi Arna,

I hope you are doing well.

Further to our earlier email and the subsequent information shared by you regarding the proposed operational structure of the business, we have carried out a further review of the potential tax implications under the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001 and the Sales Tax Act, 1990 in light of the amendments introduced through the Finance Act, 2025. Based on our present understanding, we have outlined below certain additional observations which may assist in evaluating the most appropriate structure for the business.

From an income tax perspective, as explained earlier, section 6A of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001 provides a specific taxation framework for receipts arising from the supply of digitally ordered goods or services delivered from within Pakistan through locally operated online platforms, including websites. Under this regime, tax collected at the prescribed rate is treated as final tax in terms of section 8 of the Ordinance. Accordingly, where payments are received through digital or banking channels, tax is collected at the rate of 1% of the gross amount, whereas in cases where goods are supplied on Cash on Delivery (COD) basis, the courier service collecting the payment is required to collect tax at the rate of 2% of the gross amount. The tax so collected is treated as full and final discharge of income tax liability in respect of such receipts.

On the sales tax side, the treatment depends primarily on the status of the seller under the e-commerce framework introduced through the Finance Act, 2025. Section 3(7A) of the Sales Tax Act, 1990 provides that where tax is collected and deposited by the payment intermediary or courier in respect of digitally ordered taxable goods supplied through e-commerce, such tax shall be treated as the final discharge of sales tax liability in the case of cottage industries and retailers other than Tier-1 retailers, and no input tax adjustment is allowed against those supplies. In contrast, where the supplier falls within the category of Tier-1 retailers or other registered persons operating under the normal regime, the tax withheld through e-commerce transactions is treated as adjustable against the output tax payable in the sales tax return.

Based on the information provided by you, we understand that edible oil is procured from the market by your brother’s company, after which the oil is bottled and labelled before being supplied under your brand. You had also sought our views on whether the procurement, bottling and labelling activity should be undertaken within the same SMC company that will operate the online store, or whether the SMC company should instead purchase the finished product from your brother’s company and then sell it to customers through the website.

From a tax structuring perspective, it may be more appropriate that the SMC company operating the online platform purchases the finished product from your brother’s company and subsequently sells the product to customers through the website. Under such an arrangement, the SMC company would generally be regarded as a retailer rather than a manufacturer. Provided that the company does not fall within the criteria prescribed for Tier-1 retailers under the Sales Tax Act, it would likely be treated as a retailer other than a Tier-1 retailer.

In such circumstances, the tax collected by the courier in respect of Cash on Delivery transactions at the rate prescribed for e-commerce supplies may effectively operate as the final discharge of sales tax liability on those supplies. Similarly, the income tax collected under section 6A (i.e., 1% in the case of digital payments and 2% in the case of COD transactions) would also represent the final discharge of income tax liability on the relevant receipts.

With regard to sales tax registration, it is important to note that under section 14 of the Sales Tax Act, 1990, persons making taxable supplies of goods are generally required to obtain registration with the Federal Board of Revenue. However, where a business operates purely as an online retailer and the tax on e-commerce transactions is collected by the courier or payment intermediary and treated as the final discharge of liability under section 3(7A), the practical compliance position may differ depending on the scale and nature of operations. In particular, the requirement for registration would need to be evaluated in light of the expected turnover of the business, the possibility of sales outside the e-commerce platform, and whether any of the conditions applicable to Tier-1 retailers may become relevant.

The above comments are based on our preliminary understanding of the proposed business model. Once the final operating structure, expected transaction volumes and payment mechanisms are confirmed, we will be able to provide more precise guidance regarding the applicable tax treatment and the compliance requirements under both income tax and sales tax laws.

You may kindly review the above and let us know if our understanding of the proposed arrangement is correct. We would be pleased to discuss the matter further and assist in structuring the business in a tax-efficient and compliant manner.

Kind regards,
:::

This is an important practical point to evaluate because many e-commerce businesses assume that if **courier companies or payment intermediaries are collecting tax**, then the seller may not need **sales tax registration**. The position, however, requires careful analysis under the **Sales Tax Act, 1990**.

First, the basic rule should be understood. Under **section 14 of the Sales Tax Act, 1990**, every person who makes **taxable supplies of goods in Pakistan** is required to obtain **sales tax registration** with the Federal Board of Revenue. Therefore, as a general principle, if a person is engaged in the supply of **taxable goods**, registration would normally be required.

The Finance Act 2025 introduced a specific mechanism for **e-commerce transactions** through the insertion of **section 3(7A)**. This provision states that where **digitally ordered goods are supplied through e-commerce**, and tax is **collected and deposited by the payment intermediary or courier**, such tax shall be treated as the **final discharge of sales tax liability** in the case of **cottage industries and retailers other than Tier-1 retailers**, and no input tax adjustment will be allowed against those supplies.

This effectively creates a **simplified taxation mechanism** for smaller online sellers. In such cases, the tax collected (generally **2% in case of Cash on Delivery transactions**) may operate as a **final tax**, and the seller is not required to calculate output tax or claim input tax under the normal VAT framework.

However, the requirement for **sales tax registration** depends on the overall business model.

If the seller is making **regular taxable supplies outside the e-commerce system**, for example supplying goods to distributors, wholesalers, or making offline retail sales, then **sales tax registration would generally be required**, because the seller would be operating within the normal VAT chain.

On the other hand, where a business operates **purely as an online retailer through an e-commerce platform**, does not fall within the definition of a **Tier-1 retailer**, and the tax is already being **collected by the courier or payment intermediary**, the tax so collected may effectively serve as the **final discharge of sales tax liability** on those supplies. In such a case, the practical need for registration may not arise, particularly because the seller cannot claim **input tax adjustment** under this simplified regime.

Applying this to the business structure you described earlier, where the **SMC company purchases finished oil products from your brother’s company and sells them online**, the SMC company would generally be treated as a **retailer**. Provided that it does not fall within the **Tier-1 retailer criteria** (for example, operating in large air-conditioned malls, forming part of a national chain, or exceeding the prescribed electricity consumption threshold), it would likely be categorized as a **retailer other than a Tier-1 retailer**.

In that situation, the **2% sales tax collected by the courier on Cash on Delivery transactions** may operate as the **final discharge of sales tax liability** on those e-commerce supplies.

That said, before reaching a definitive conclusion, three practical factors usually need to be confirmed:

• the expected **annual turnover of the business**,  
• whether the business will make **sales outside the e-commerce platform**, and  
• whether any of the **Tier-1 retailer conditions** may apply.

These factors ultimately determine whether the business can operate under the **simplified e-commerce withholding regime** or whether it must enter the **regular sales tax registration and reporting framework** under the Sales Tax Act, 1990.

What the provision is essentially doing is **creating two different sales tax treatments for e-commerce vendors**, depending on the nature and size of the seller.

First, the law introduces **section 3(7A) of the Sales Tax Act, 1990**, which deals specifically with **digitally ordered goods sold through e-commerce platforms** where tax is collected by **payment intermediaries or courier companies**.

The provision then splits vendors into two broad categories.

**1. Cottage industry and retailers other than Tier-1 retailers**

For these smaller businesses, the tax that is **collected and deposited by the payment intermediary or courier** is treated as the **final discharge of their sales tax liability** on those supplies.

This means three important things in practical terms:

- The seller does **not need to calculate further output tax** on those supplies.
- The tax already deducted in the e-commerce transaction **settles the liability**.
- **No input tax adjustment is allowed** against those supplies.

So effectively, for small retailers and cottage industries selling goods online, the system operates almost like a **simplified final tax mechanism**, where compliance is handled through the intermediary.

The law then defines **cottage industry** very specifically. A manufacturer will fall under this category only if **all four conditions** are satisfied:

• no industrial gas or electricity connection  
• located in a residential area  
• labour force not exceeding **10 workers**  
• annual turnover **not exceeding Rs. 8 million**

If any one of these conditions is not met, the business cannot claim cottage industry status.

**2. All other persons (including Tier-1 retailers)**

For larger businesses, the treatment is completely different.

If the seller falls into this category — for example a **Tier-1 retailer or a normal registered supplier** — then the tax collected by the courier or payment intermediary is **not final tax**.

Instead:

- Sales tax must be calculated under the **normal sales tax regime**.
- The tax withheld in e-commerce transactions becomes **adjustable tax**.
- The seller must report the **full output tax in the sales tax return** and adjust the withheld amount against it.

This means the seller can still **claim input tax** and operate under the standard VAT-type mechanism of the Sales Tax Act.

The law then defines **Tier-1 retailers**, which are generally **large or organized retail businesses**. A retailer will fall into this category if any of the following conditions are met:

• operating as part of a **national or international chain store**  
• operating in an **air-conditioned shopping mall or plaza** (except kiosks)  
• cumulative electricity bill in the last 12 months exceeds **Rs. 600,000**  
• functioning as a **wholesaler-cum-retailer importing goods and selling both wholesale and retail**

So the design of the law is quite deliberate:  
**small sellers are given a simplified final tax treatment**, while **larger organized retailers must remain within the full sales tax system**.

In practical advisory work, the real challenge usually arises in **correctly determining whether an e-commerce seller qualifies as a Tier-1 retailer or not**, because that classification directly determines whether the **tax deducted in e-commerce is final or merely adjustable**. That classification point is often where disputes with the tax authorities begin.

I have read the provision.

The clause defines **“cottage industry”** under the tax law as a **small-scale manufacturing concern** that must satisfy **all four conditions simultaneously**. The conditions essentially ensure that the activity remains **very small, home-based, and non-industrial in nature**.

First, the manufacturing concern **must not have an industrial gas or electricity connection**. This condition indicates that the activity is not operating as a formal industrial unit. If the business uses a commercial or industrial electricity connection, it would generally fall outside this definition.

Second, the unit **must be located in a residential area**. The idea behind this condition is that the activity is carried out in a household or small premises rather than in an industrial zone or factory setup.

Third, the **total labour force must not exceed ten workers**. This threshold is used to distinguish cottage-level production from larger small or medium-scale manufacturing units.

Fourth, the **annual turnover from all supplies must not exceed eight million rupees**. The turnover limit ensures that once the business grows beyond a certain economic scale, it no longer qualifies as a cottage industry for tax purposes.

The key point in interpreting this clause is that **all four conditions must be met together**. If even one condition is not satisfied—for example, if the business has an industrial electricity connection or its turnover exceeds the prescribed limit—the entity would **not qualify as a cottage industry under the law**.

Further to our earlier email outlining the preliminary income tax and sales tax implications of the proposed e-commerce business model, we have also evaluated the possible sales tax treatment under two different operational structures. For clarity, we have briefly outlined below the two possible options so that the overall tax impact and compliance requirements may be considered before finalizing the operating model.

**Option 1 – Procurement and Sales through the SMC Company (Normal Sales Tax Regime)**

Under this option, the procurement of oil and other materials as well as the sale of finished products would be undertaken by the SMC company itself. The SMC company would purchase oil and related inputs directly and sell the finished product to customers through the online platform. The bottling, labeling and related processing activities may continue to be performed by the existing sole proprietorship as a toll manufacturing arrangement.

In such a case, the sole proprietorship would charge conversion or processing charges to the SMC company for bottling and labeling services. These processing services would be subject to sales tax at the standard rate of 18%.

Under this structure, the SMC company would be required to obtain sales tax registration and operate under the normal sales tax regime. The company would be able to claim input tax adjustment on the sales tax charged on purchases of oil and other materials as well as on the conversion or processing charges billed by the sole proprietorship.

When the finished product is supplied to customers, the SMC company would charge sales tax at the standard rate of 18% on the retail value of the product. In the case of e-commerce transactions, the courier company may deduct tax at the prescribed rate (currently 2%) on Cash on Delivery transactions. Such deduction would be treated as adjustable tax and would be available as a credit against the output tax liability of the SMC company. After adjusting the available input tax and the tax deducted by the courier company, the remaining sales tax payable, if any, would be discharged by the SMC company through its monthly sales tax return.

**Option 2 – Manufacturing and Supply through the Sole Proprietorship (Simplified E-Commerce Regime)**

Under the second option, the existing structure would largely remain unchanged. The sole proprietorship operated by your brother would continue to procure oil from the market, undertake bottling and labeling activities, and supply the finished product. The sole proprietorship would obtain sales tax registration and charge sales tax at the standard rate of 18% on the finished product supplied to the SMC company.

The SMC company, in this scenario, would function primarily as an online retailer selling the finished product to end consumers through the website. As discussed earlier, under the e-commerce provisions introduced through section 3(7A) of the Sales Tax Act, 1990, where a supplier operates as a retailer other than a Tier-1 retailer and tax is collected by the courier or payment intermediary, such tax may operate as the final discharge of sales tax liability and input tax adjustment may not be available.

Consequently, the sales tax charged by the sole proprietorship on the supply of finished goods to the SMC company would effectively become part of the cost of the product for the SMC company. The SMC company would recover the applicable 2% tax on Cash on Delivery transactions from customers, which would be collected by the courier company and deposited with the government.

One practical advantage of this structure is that the SMC company may not be required to obtain sales tax registration or file monthly sales tax returns, as the sales tax obligations would largely remain with the sole proprietorship. However, the corresponding drawback is that the input tax embedded in the supply chain — including sales tax charged on the procurement of oil, packaging material and other inputs — would ultimately become part of the cost of the finished product from the perspective of the SMC company.

In light of the above, it would be advisable to evaluate both options by considering the overall supply chain, particularly the extent of input tax embedded in the procurement of oil and other materials from the local market. If a significant amount of sales tax is being charged in the upstream supply chain, operating under the normal sales tax regime through the SMC company may allow recovery of such input tax through adjustment. Conversely, if the embedded input tax is relatively low, the simplified e-commerce mechanism under the second option may provide a more straightforward compliance approach.

You may wish to review the above alternatives and consider which structure appears more practical and commercially viable for your operations. We would be pleased to discuss these options further and assist in structuring the arrangement in the most tax-efficient manner.

Thank you for sharing the background and the document. I have reviewed both your email and the order circulated by Magnus.

At the outset, it appears that the position currently being taken by Magnus’ tax advisor is based on the principle that expenses relating to a **separate fund or investment vehicle should ordinarily be borne by the fund itself rather than by the sponsoring or related company**. The document shared by them also reflects a similar regulatory thinking. In that case, the tax authorities rejected an amendment in the rules of an Employees’ Provident Fund where the **company intended to bear the expenses of the fund**, primarily on the basis that such arrangement would allow the company to claim the expenditure in its own accounts and thereby reduce its taxable income. The tax authority specifically observed that if the company bears expenses that actually belong to the fund, the company would claim deductions against its profits, which was considered inappropriate from a tax perspective. fileciteturn0file0

Keeping the above principle in view, the core issue in your case is whether the **fund management services provided by Magnus are rendered to Wafi Energy Pakistan Limited or to the investment fund itself**.

If the investment portfolio or fund is legally maintained **in the name of Wafi Energy and forms part of the company’s own treasury or investment management activity**, then Magnus is effectively providing services to Wafi Energy. In that situation:

- The invoice being issued on **Wafi Energy’s NTN** would be commercially and legally appropriate.  
- Wafi would be entitled to record the expense in its books.  
- Correspondingly, the **Sindh Sales Tax charged by Magnus could legitimately be claimed as input tax** (subject to the normal input tax admissibility rules under the Sindh Sales Tax on Services Act, 2011).

However, if the investment structure is such that **the fund is a separate legal or identifiable entity (for example a managed fund, trust structure, or segregated portfolio maintained under a different NTN)** and Magnus is actually managing that fund rather than Wafi itself, then the expense technically belongs to the fund. In that situation:

- The **service recipient is the fund**, not Wafi Energy.  
- The invoice should be issued on the **fund’s NTN**.  
- The cost should ideally be **paid out of the fund account**, not the company’s operating account.  
- Consequently, **input tax would also belong to the fund**, and Wafi should generally not claim that input tax.

From a tax compliance perspective, the tax authorities typically examine **the actual beneficiary of the service** rather than the payment channel alone. If the service relates to management of assets that legally belong to the fund, continuing to route the expense through Wafi may create questions during a sales tax audit or income tax assessment regarding the admissibility of the expense and the input tax claim.

Therefore, the correct treatment ultimately depends on the **legal ownership and structure of the investment fund** and the **service agreement executed with Magnus**. If Magnus’ contract clearly states that they are managing the fund itself, their current position of invoicing the **fund NTN** is technically more aligned with standard tax treatment.

Before giving a final view, it would be useful to briefly review the following documents:

1. The **Investment Management Agreement** executed with Magnus.  
2. Whether the **fund is registered or maintained under a separate NTN**.  
3. How the **investments are recorded in Wafi’s financial statements** (direct treasury investments vs. fund structure).

Once these are reviewed, we can confirm conclusively whether the earlier practice of issuing invoices on Wafi’s NTN and claiming input tax was technically sustainable or whether the revised approach suggested by Magnus should be adopted going forward.

If you could share the **agreement with Magnus and the structure of the fund**, I can revert with a more definitive position.

Company کا بنیادی موقف یہ ہے کہ:

- assessment officer نے **change of opinion** کی بنیاد پر amendment کیا۔

**Legal reasoning**

Income Tax Ordinance کے تحت:

Section 122 صرف اسی صورت میں استعمال ہو سکتا ہے جب:

- **definite information available ہو**  
- یا **mistake apparent ہو**

اگر اصل assessment کے وقت facts already record پر تھے تو بعد میں amendment **ultra vires** ہو سکتا ہے۔

اگر audit selection prescribed procedure کے بغیر ہو تو subsequent proceedings بھی questionable ہو جاتی ہیں۔

Tribunal کے متعدد فیصلوں میں:

- **non-selection in balloting**
- **mechanical audit initiation**

# 2. Legal Framework of the Dispute

Before evaluating each issue, it is necessary to understand the statutory provisions involved.

### Section 122 – Amendment of Assessment

Section 122 empowers the Commissioner to amend an assessment where:

- **definite information has come into possession**, or  
- **there is a mistake apparent from the record**.

However, it is settled law that this provision **cannot be used merely to change the earlier opinion of the assessing officer**.

---

### Section 177 – Audit of Taxpayer

Section 177 authorizes the Commissioner to conduct an audit of a taxpayer’s records.

However, after the introduction of **section 214C**, audit selection was required to be made through **computer balloting** unless otherwise authorized.

---

### Section 21 – Disallowance of Expenditure

Section 21 specifies certain expenditures which are **not deductible** while computing business income.

Relevant provisions include:

- **Section 21(c)** – disallowance for payments made without deduction of withholding tax where such deduction was required.

---

### Section 109 – Recharacterization of Transactions

Section 109 allows the Commissioner to recharacterize a transaction where the transaction:

- has **no commercial substance**, or  
- has been structured primarily to **avoid tax**.

---

### Section 113 – Minimum Tax on Turnover

Section 113 imposes a **minimum tax on turnover**, which operates as a **fallback tax mechanism** where the tax payable under the normal regime is less than the prescribed percentage of turnover.

However, the concerned financial institutions have indicated that, due to the significant passage of time, **records from the inception of the accounts are no longer available in their systems**. Consequently, obtaining **complete bank statements from the original inception of the accounts**, as requested in the notice, is not practically feasible at this stage.

As explained therein, the foreign bank accounts represent **historic savings accumulated by the late Mr. Ali Gohar during his employment abroad**, including his tenure with Singapore Airlines. The deposits in these accounts were made many years ago and the accounts have remained **dormant and inactive for more than a decade**, with no fresh deposits, investments, or transactional activity during the recent tax years under review.

In these circumstances, the proposed action under section 122 read with section 111 of the Ordinance is not sustainable in law. The transactions in question clearly fall within the well-established principle of **“past and closed transactions”**, and the statutory limitation prescribed under section 122(2) of the Ordinance operates as a complete bar against reopening matters relating to deposits made more than fifteen years ago.

In this regard, reliance has already been placed in the earlier submission on the judgment of the **Honourable Appellate Tribunal Inland Revenue, Lahore Bench in the case of *Mian Amer Rashid (ITA No. 1097/LB/2024, decided on March 21, 2024)*.** In the said decision, the Tribunal categorically held that foreign bank balances originating from historic deposits, where no fresh inflow or investment occurred during the relevant tax year, cannot be treated as unexplained income under section 111 of the Ordinance.

The Tribunal further observed that once the statutory limitation period expires, the taxpayer acquires a **vested right in the finality of past assessments**, and such closed transactions cannot be revived merely because information regarding those accounts later becomes available through mechanisms such as the **OECD’s Automatic Exchange of Information (AEOI)**.

Similarly, reliance was also placed on the decision of the Honourable Appellate Tribunal Inland Revenue in the case of **Mian Tauqeer Aslam v. CIR**, wherein it was held that section 111(2)(ii), even after the amendment introduced through the Finance Act, 2018, cannot be applied retrospectively to bring to tax foreign assets acquired many years earlier where the statutory time limit for initiating proceedings had already expired. The Tribunal emphasized that once the limitation period lapses, the taxpayer acquires a vested right that such historic transactions cannot subsequently be reopened.

The above judicial precedents clearly establish that the **mere existence of historic foreign bank balances does not constitute a taxable event in a later tax year**, particularly in the absence of any fresh investment or transaction during the relevant period.

In the present case, the factual position remains undisputed: the deposits in the offshore accounts were made many years ago, primarily between **2005 and 2009**, and no new deposits or investments have been made in the recent tax years under review. Accordingly, the invocation of section 111 of the Ordinance in the present circumstances is legally untenable and contrary to the settled jurisprudence of the appellate forums.

Notwithstanding the above legal position, the undersigned reiterates full cooperation with the proceedings and remains willing to provide any additional explanation or documentation that may reasonably be available. The requested documents, including the **death certificate of Mr. Ali Gohar and evidence establishing the relationship**, will be placed on record during the hearing before your good office.

In view of the above facts and settled legal principles, it is respectfully submitted that the proceedings initiated under section 122(9) read with section 111 of the Ordinance are **without lawful authority and not sustainable in law**. It is therefore respectfully requested that the explanations already placed on record may kindly be considered in their true legal and factual perspective and the proceedings initiated through the present notices may kindly be dropped.

When you go before the **SRB Appellate Tribunal**, the written grounds are only the starting point. What actually persuades the bench are the **hearing grounds**—the structured oral arguments that show why the demand under the **Sindh Sales Tax on Services Act, 2011 (SSTSA)** cannot legally survive. Think of it as guiding the Tribunal step-by-step: jurisdiction first, charging provision second, factual misinterpretation third.

Below is a **refined set of hearing grounds / arguments** that can be used during the Tribunal hearing in the PICTL matter.

---

### 1. Lack of Legislative Competence – Port Operations Fall Within Federal Domain
The first and most fundamental argument is that the services rendered by the appellant arise directly from its role as a **container terminal operator within a federally regulated port**. Ports declared by law to be federal ports fall under **Entry 53 of the Federal Legislative List in the Fourth Schedule to the Constitution**.  

The terminal operations carried out by the appellant—such as container handling, loading and unloading, and terminal infrastructure operations—are integral components of port operations. Since the Constitution assigns legislative competence over such matters to the Federation, the provincial legislature cannot impose sales tax on services that are inherently part of port operations.  

Accordingly, the levy of Sindh Sales Tax on such services is **constitutionally unsustainable**.

---

### 2. Scope of Tax Under SSTSA 2011 Is Limited to Taxable Services
Under **section 3 of the Sindh Sales Tax on Services Act, 2011**, sales tax is chargeable only on **taxable services specified in the Second Schedule**.  

The department has attempted to bring the appellant’s activities within the taxable scope without properly establishing that the services actually fall within the relevant service entry. A charging provision in a taxing statute must be **strictly interpreted**, and unless the service clearly falls within the taxable category, no tax liability can be imposed.

Therefore, the demand lacks a proper statutory foundation.

---

### 3. Misinterpretation of Rule 40 of the Sindh Sales Tax Rules
The department has relied on **Rule 40 of the Sindh Sales Tax Rules, 2011** to support the levy. However, a proper reading of the rule shows that the taxable scope primarily relates to **services provided in relation to imported cargo**.

The appellant’s operations include handling of both **import and export containers**, as well as terminal infrastructure services. By treating all terminal activities as taxable services under Rule 40, the department has incorrectly expanded the scope of the rule beyond what the law permits.

Accordingly, the interpretation adopted by the department is legally flawed.

---

### 4. Services Relating to Export Cargo Are Not Taxable in the Manner Alleged
A significant portion of the appellant’s operations relate to **export cargo movement through the terminal**. The legislative framework distinguishes between services relating to imported cargo and export cargo.  

The department has ignored this distinction and treated all terminal handling activities as taxable. Such an approach is inconsistent with the scheme of the rules and results in an **incorrect expansion of the tax base**.

---

### 5. Handling of Empty Containers Cannot Be Treated as Cargo Handling
The impugned demand also includes services relating to **movement and handling of empty containers**. In port operations, empty containers represent **shipping equipment repositioning** rather than cargo.

Therefore, treating empty container handling as taxable cargo-related services is factually and legally incorrect. The impugned order fails to distinguish between **cargo movement and container logistics**, leading to an inflated tax demand.

---

### 6. Composite Nature of Terminal Operations Ignored
The appellant operates a **container terminal under a concession arrangement**, providing integrated infrastructure and operational services within the port area. These activities constitute **composite terminal operations** rather than isolated taxable services.

The department has artificially segregated components of these operations and attempted to treat them as independent taxable services. Such artificial splitting of composite services is contrary to established principles of tax interpretation.

---

### 7. Absence of Any Intentional Default
Even if, arguendo, the Tribunal were to consider any portion of the services taxable, the imposition of **penalty and default surcharge** remains unjustified.  

The issue involved in the present case is clearly one of **interpretation of law and classification of services**, and the appellant has acted in good faith based on its understanding of the applicable legal framework. Accordingly, no element of willful default or suppression exists that would justify the imposition of penalties.

---

### 8. Impugned Order Fails to Properly Address Appellant’s Submissions
During appellate proceedings, the appellant placed detailed factual and legal submissions before the learned Commissioner (Appeals). However, the impugned order does not adequately address those submissions and instead confirms the assessment largely by reiterating the position adopted by the assessing authority.

Such an approach reflects **non-application of mind** and renders the order unsustainable.

- wording of the amendment

## 7. Penalty and Default Surcharge Ground is Weak
The penalty ground says:

> no mens rea established.

That principle normally applies in **income tax penalty cases**.

Under **sales tax laws**, penalties often arise on:

- **incorrect declaration**

even without mens rea.

Therefore this ground is relatively weak unless you show:

- the issue involved **interpretational dispute**

The argument should therefore be reframed as:

instead of only **mens rea**.

PICTL’s operations typically include multiple revenue streams such as:

- port infrastructure access

The appeal should argue that **SRB has incorrectly treated composite services as taxable services** without proper classification.

This argument is **currently missing**.

The prayer currently asks to:

> set aside the impugned order.

It should also request:

- **deletion of the entire tax demand**
- **cancellation of penalty and default surcharge**
- **any consequential relief**

Tribunals prefer **specific relief wording**.

Only **one case (2017 PTD 01)** is cited.

For a dispute of **Rs. 245 million**, the appeal should ideally rely on:

*(Before the Appellate Tribunal under the Sindh Sales Tax on Services Act, 2011)*

2. **That the learned Commissioner (Appeals) has erred in law in upholding the levy of Sindh Sales Tax on services which essentially relate to the operations of a federally regulated port.** The activities carried out by the appellant are integral to port operations and fall within the domain of matters relating to ports as provided under **Entry 53 of the Federal Legislative List in the Fourth Schedule to the Constitution of the Islamic Republic of Pakistan**. Consequently, the levy of provincial sales tax on such activities is without lawful authority.

3. **That the learned Commissioner (Appeals) failed to appreciate that the scope of taxation under the Act does not extend to services which constitutionally fall within the Federal Legislative List.** The constitutional framework clearly demarcates the legislative competence of the Federation and the Provinces, and any attempt to levy provincial sales tax on services integrally connected with federal port operations is ultra vires the Constitution.

4. **That the learned Commissioner (Appeals) further failed to consider that the Explanation inserted in section 3 of the Act through subsequent amendments clarifies that services relating to matters enumerated in the Federal Legislative List fall outside the scope of provincial sales taxation.** The said clarification is declaratory and clarificatory in nature and therefore reinforces the position that the impugned levy could not legally be imposed on the services rendered by the appellant.

5. **That the learned Commissioner (Appeals) erred in law and on facts in misinterpreting the scope of Rule 40 of the Sindh Sales Tax Rules, 2011.** A proper reading of the said rule indicates that the taxability contemplated therein pertains only to services relating to **imported cargo**, whereas the services rendered by the appellant also relate to export cargo and other terminal operations which fall outside the ambit of the said rule.

6. **That the learned Commissioner (Appeals) failed to appreciate that services relating to export cargo cannot be subjected to the levy in the manner adopted by the assessing authority.** The legislative scheme underlying the taxation of port-related services clearly differentiates between services relating to imported cargo and those relating to export cargo, and the impugned order has ignored this distinction.

7. **That the learned Commissioner (Appeals) also erred in treating handling of empty containers as services relating to cargo.** Empty containers do not constitute cargo; rather they represent shipping equipment repositioning within the terminal operations. Consequently, the inclusion of such activities within the taxable base is legally unsustainable and contrary to the factual nature of the services rendered.

8. **That the learned Commissioner (Appeals) failed to properly examine the composite and integrated nature of the appellant’s terminal operations.** The appellant provides integrated terminal infrastructure and operational facilities under a port concession arrangement, and the impugned order erroneously isolates certain activities and treats them as independently taxable services without proper legal basis.

9. **That the proceedings initiated by the assessing authority and subsequently upheld by the learned Commissioner (Appeals) suffer from jurisdictional defects as the underlying services do not fall within the charging framework of the Act.** Consequently, the entire demand created through the impugned order is without lawful authority.

10. **That the imposition of penalty and default surcharge is also unjustified and liable to be deleted.** The issues involved in the present matter relate to interpretation of law and classification of services, and therefore no element of willful default or deliberate suppression can be attributed to the appellant.

11. **That the learned Commissioner (Appeals) failed to properly appreciate the factual submissions and documentary evidence placed on record by the appellant and upheld the assessment without adequately addressing the substantive legal and factual contentions raised during appellate proceedings.**

12. **That the impugned order is otherwise arbitrary, unreasonable and liable to be set aside on any other grounds which may be urged at the time of hearing.**

The draft grounds focus heavily on **procedural irregularities (ex-parte order, hearing attendance, etc.)**, but the **core issue of taxability under SSTSA 2011** does not appear to be articulated strongly.

The appeal grounds should clearly argue:

The grounds should **specifically rebut the reasoning adopted by the Commissioner Appeals**, such as:

Strong Tribunal appeals normally include **alternative grounds**, such as:

Although the draft mentions the **ex-parte nature of the order**, the argument could be strengthened by stating that:

We refer to your notice bearing barcode No. 100000272559437 dated March 5, 2026, issued under section 120(3) of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001, whereby certain deficiencies have been identified in the return of income filed by our above-mentioned client for subject tax year.

یہ سوال بالکل تکنیکی ہے اور اکثر practitioners کو یہی confusion ہوتی ہے، کیونکہ **“unabsorbed depreciation”** کی اصطلاح پاکستان کے **Income Tax Ordinance, 2001** میں explicitly defined term کے طور پر نہیں دی گئی۔ قانون اس concept کو براہِ راست define نہیں کرتا بلکہ یہ **statutory interpretation اور computation mechanism** سے derive ہوتا ہے۔

اس کو step-by-step سمجھتے ہیں۔

سب سے پہلے **Section 18** کو دیکھیں۔ یہ provision کہتا ہے کہ **“Income from Business”** وہ profits and gains ہیں جو taxpayer نے business سے earn کیے ہوں اور جن کو Ordinance کے مطابق compute کیا جائے۔ اس کا مطلب یہ ہے کہ business income compute کرتے وقت تمام allowable deductions apply ہوں گی۔

ان allowable deductions میں سے ایک **depreciation allowance** ہے جو **Section 22** کے تحت allow ہوتی ہے۔ Section 22(1) کے مطابق اگر کوئی **depreciable asset business میں استعمال ہو رہا ہو** تو taxpayer اس asset پر depreciation claim کر سکتا ہے۔ اس depreciation کی calculation **Part I of the Third Schedule** کے مطابق ہوتی ہے۔

اب اصل بات یہاں آتی ہے۔

Section 22 depreciation کو ایک **deduction** کے طور پر allow کرتا ہے، لیکن Ordinance یہ کہیں نہیں کہتا کہ اگر depreciation income سے زیادہ ہو جائے تو اس excess کو business loss treat کیا جائے۔ یعنی قانون depreciation کو **operational loss میں convert نہیں کرتا**۔

اس لئے computation logically اس طرح ہوتی ہے:

اگر business income depreciation سے پہلے **positive** ہے تو depreciation اس income کو **reduce کر کے zero تک لے جا سکتی ہے** لیکن اس سے آگے جا کر **business loss create نہیں کرتی**۔

اس کا مطلب یہ ہے کہ depreciation کا وہ حصہ جو current year میں adjust نہیں ہو سکا وہ simply **future years کے depreciation deduction کا حصہ بن جاتا ہے**۔

اسی remaining amount کو tax practice میں **“unabsorbed depreciation”** کہا جاتا ہے۔

یہ terminology پاکستان کے tax law میں **express definition کے طور پر نہیں بلکہ judicial and administrative interpretation کے ذریعے** استعمال ہوتی ہے۔ FBR کے computation formats، tax commentaries اور professional practice میں بھی اسی اصطلاح کو استعمال کیا جاتا ہے۔

اس کو ایک simple numerical example سے سمجھیں۔

فرض کریں:

Business income before depreciation = Rs. 100  
Depreciation allowance under Section 22 = Rs. 200  

Computation اس طرح ہوگی:

Income before depreciation = 100  
Less: Depreciation = 200  

Taxable income = Nil

یہاں Rs.100 depreciation adjust ہو گیا۔ باقی **Rs.100 depreciation adjust نہیں ہو سکا**۔

یہ Rs.100 **business loss نہیں بنے گا** کیونکہ company operationally loss میں نہیں تھی۔ اس لئے یہ Rs.100 future years میں **depreciation deduction carry forward** ہو جائے گا۔ یہی amount practical language میں **unabsorbed depreciation** کہلاتی ہے۔

اب اس کو **business loss** سے compare کریں۔

اگر business result depreciation سے پہلے ہی **negative** ہو، مثلاً:

Business loss before depreciation = Rs.100  

تو یہ **business loss** ہوگا اور اس کا treatment **Section 57 (Carry Forward of Business Loss)** کے تحت ہوگا۔ Section 57 کے مطابق business losses کو future business income کے خلاف set-off کیا جا سکتا ہے لیکن عام طور پر **maximum six tax years** تک carry forward کیا جا سکتا ہے۔

اس لئے Ordinance میں دو الگ concepts موجود ہیں:

پہلا **business loss** جو **Section 57** کے تحت governed ہوتا ہے۔

دوسرا **depreciation allowance under Section 22** جو اگر current year میں absorb نہ ہو سکے تو future years میں deduction کے طور پر continue رہتا ہے، جسے practice میں **unabsorbed depreciation** کہا جاتا ہے۔

مختصر طور پر:

• **Section 22** depreciation allowance provide کرتا ہے  
• **Section 18** business income computation کا framework دیتا ہے  
• **Section 57** business losses کے carry forward کو govern کرتا ہے  

اور انہی provisions کو together پڑھنے سے یہ principle نکلتا ہے کہ **excess depreciation business loss نہیں بنتا بلکہ depreciation allowance carried forward بن جاتا ہے** جسے tax practice میں **unabsorbed depreciation** کہا جاتا ہے۔

اگر آپ چاہیں تو میں آپ کو یہ بھی explain کر سکتا ہوں کہ **پاکستان کے courts اور appellate tribunals نے اس concept کو کیسے interpret کیا ہے** اور کیوں اکثر assessments میں **business loss اور unabsorbed depreciation کو mix کر کے غلط computation کر دی جاتی ہے**۔ یہ litigation میں ایک بہت common technical point بنتا ہے۔

**Subject:** Clarification on Treatment of Depreciation, Unabsorbed Depreciation and Business Loss under the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001

Dear [Client Name],

Further to our **discussion yesterday**, you sought our views regarding the correct tax treatment of depreciation where the depreciation allowance exceeds the taxable income of the company, particularly in the context of determining whether the resulting amount should be treated as a **taxable loss** or **unabsorbed depreciation** for the purposes of the **Income Tax Ordinance, 2001 (the “Ordinance”)**. During the discussion, the understanding appeared to be that if depreciation exceeds taxable income, the resulting negative figure may represent a **taxable loss**. Upon further technical evaluation of the relevant provisions of the Ordinance, we consider it appropriate to clarify the correct legal position, as the treatment requires a distinction between **business loss** and **unabsorbed depreciation**.

Under the scheme of the Ordinance, the computation of income from business is governed by **section 18**, which provides that the income chargeable under the head **“Income from Business”** shall be the profits and gains of a person’s business for the tax year. In determining such profits or gains, the Ordinance permits various deductions, including depreciation, which is specifically governed by **section 22 of the Ordinance**.

Section 22(1) provides that a person is entitled to a **depreciation deduction for the tax year for any depreciable asset used in the person’s business** during that year. The depreciation deduction is computed in accordance with the rates and rules prescribed in **Part I of the Third Schedule to the Ordinance**. Accordingly, depreciation is treated as an allowable deduction in computing taxable income from business.

However, the Ordinance recognizes that in certain cases the depreciation allowance may exceed the income available for adjustment in a particular tax year. In such circumstances, the treatment of the excess amount is governed by **section 22(8) of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001**, which provides that where the depreciation deduction allowed to a person for a tax year **exceeds the person’s income from business for that year**, the excess amount shall be **treated as unabsorbed depreciation** and carried forward to the next tax year.

Therefore, the Ordinance creates a specific statutory mechanism whereby the excess depreciation does not convert into a business loss. Instead, the law preserves the character of that excess amount as **unabsorbed depreciation**, which continues to be carried forward for adjustment in future tax years.

To illustrate this position, consider the following example:

Suppose the company has **taxable income before depreciation of Rs. 100**, while the depreciation allowable under section 22 amounts to **Rs. 200**.

In this case, the depreciation deduction will first be adjusted against the available income of Rs. 100. Consequently, the taxable income for the year will be reduced to **nil**. The remaining **Rs. 100**, representing the portion of depreciation that could not be absorbed during the year, will not be treated as a business loss. Instead, in accordance with **section 22(8) of the Ordinance**, it will be classified as **unabsorbed depreciation**.

This unabsorbed depreciation is then carried forward to subsequent tax years and may be deducted against future income from business when such income arises.

It is important to distinguish this position from the treatment of **business losses**, which are governed separately under **section 57 of the Ordinance**. Section 57 provides that where a person sustains a **loss under the head “Income from Business”** in a tax year, that loss may be carried forward and set off against income from business in subsequent years, subject to certain conditions and limitations. One of the key restrictions is that **business losses may generally be carried forward for a period of six tax years** immediately succeeding the tax year in which the loss was sustained.

Accordingly, the Ordinance treats **unabsorbed depreciation and business losses as two distinct categories**, each governed by separate provisions and carry-forward rules.

For clarity, it is useful to consider a second scenario.

Suppose that before considering depreciation, the company already has a **taxable loss from business operations**, for example **negative Rs. 100**, and the allowable depreciation for the year is **Rs. 200**.

In such a situation, the loss arising from business operations represents a **business loss under section 57**, which may be carried forward subject to the statutory limitations applicable to business losses. The depreciation deduction will continue to retain its character as depreciation, and to the extent it cannot be absorbed in the relevant year, it will be treated as **unabsorbed depreciation under section 22(8)** and carried forward accordingly.

In other words, the Ordinance does not merge depreciation into business losses; rather, the law maintains the **separate identity of unabsorbed depreciation and business loss**, each governed by its own carry-forward mechanism.

Another important practical aspect is that **unabsorbed depreciation may generally be carried forward for an indefinite period until fully absorbed**, provided that the taxpayer continues to derive income from business against which the allowance may be set off. This treatment distinguishes it from business losses under section 57, which are subject to the **six-year carry-forward limitation**.

Based on the above analysis of **sections 18, 22 and 57 of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001**, the correct legal position may therefore be summarized as follows:

Where taxable income before depreciation is positive but depreciation exceeds that income, the income will first be reduced to **nil**, and the excess depreciation will be treated as **unabsorbed depreciation under section 22(8)** rather than as a business loss.

Conversely, where the taxpayer already has a loss from business operations before depreciation is considered, that amount will be treated as a **business loss under section 57**, while any depreciation that cannot be absorbed will remain **unabsorbed depreciation**, to be carried forward separately.

This distinction is particularly important for tax planning, forecasting future tax positions, and determining the availability of deductions in subsequent tax years.

Please feel free to reach out should you wish to discuss how this treatment may affect the tax position of the **group entities**, particularly in the context of projected profitability and the utilization of carried-forward deductions in future years.

Kind regards,  
[Your Name]

**Subject:** Treatment of Unabsorbed Depreciation under the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001

Dear [Client Name],

I hope you are doing well.

Further to our recent discussion, we would like to clarify the treatment of depreciation where the depreciation claim exceeds the taxable income for a particular tax year under the provisions of the **Income Tax Ordinance, 2001 (the “Ordinance”)**.

For ease of understanding, let us consider a simple illustration. Suppose the taxable income of a company **before claiming depreciation and amortization** is **Rs. 100**, while the admissible depreciation for the year amounts to **Rs. 200**.

Under the scheme of the Ordinance, depreciation is allowed as a deductible expense in computing income from business under **section 22**, read with the relevant provisions governing computation of business income. When the depreciation allowance exceeds the income available for adjustment in the relevant tax year, the law does **not treat the excess portion as a taxable loss in the conventional sense**.

Instead, the Ordinance treats the remaining unadjusted amount as **“unabsorbed depreciation.”**

In the above illustration, the depreciation of **Rs. 200** would first be adjusted against the available income of **Rs. 100**, thereby reducing the taxable income for the year to **nil**. The remaining **Rs. 100** (i.e., depreciation that could not be absorbed during the year) would be treated as **unabsorbed depreciation**.

It is important to note that this amount is **not classified as a “taxable accumulated loss” or business loss** under the Ordinance. Rather, it retains its character as **depreciation allowance carried forward**.

The significance of this distinction is important from a tax-computation perspective. **Unabsorbed depreciation may be carried forward and adjusted against future taxable business income**, subject to the relevant provisions of the Ordinance. Unlike normal business losses, which are governed by specific carry-forward limitations under **section 57**, unabsorbed depreciation generally continues to be available for adjustment in subsequent years until fully absorbed, provided the taxpayer continues to derive income from business.

Therefore, in the scenario discussed above, the correct tax treatment would be that **Rs. 100 of depreciation is absorbed in the current year**, while the **remaining Rs. 100 represents unabsorbed depreciation carried forward**, and not a taxable accumulated loss.

This distinction is important for future tax computations, minimum tax considerations, and overall tax planning.

Should you require, we would be pleased to further discuss how this treatment interacts with **minimum tax provisions, carried-forward business losses, and group tax planning**, as these areas often create practical implications in corporate tax computations.

Kind regards,  
[Your Name]

**Subject:** Clarification on Treatment of Excess Depreciation and Business Loss under the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001  

Dear [Client Name],  

Further to our discussion yesterday, you had sought our views regarding the correct tax treatment under the **Income Tax Ordinance, 2001 (the “Ordinance”)** in a situation where the depreciation allowance exceeds the taxable income of a company, particularly whether the resulting amount should be treated as a **taxable loss** or as **unabsorbed depreciation**.

During the course of our discussion, it appeared that where depreciation exceeds taxable income, the net negative figure may be treated as a **taxable loss**. Upon revisiting the relevant provisions of the Ordinance, we consider it appropriate to clarify the correct legal position, as the law distinguishes between **business losses** and **unabsorbed depreciation**, and both are governed by separate provisions and carry-forward mechanisms.

Under the scheme of the Ordinance, the computation of income from business is governed by **section 18**, which provides that the income chargeable under the head **“Income from Business”** shall be the profits and gains derived by a person from any business carried on during the tax year. In computing such income, deductions are allowed in accordance with the provisions of the Ordinance, including depreciation on depreciable assets used in the business.

The allowance of depreciation is specifically governed by **section 22 of the Ordinance**, which entitles a taxpayer to claim a **depreciation deduction for depreciable assets used in the business during the tax year**, computed in accordance with the rates and rules prescribed in **Part I of the Third Schedule to the Ordinance**.

However, the Ordinance does not treat excess depreciation as a business loss. Instead, where the depreciation deduction cannot be fully absorbed against the business income of the relevant year, the unadjusted portion continues to retain its character as **depreciation allowance available for adjustment in subsequent tax years**. In practice, this remaining portion is commonly referred to as **“unabsorbed depreciation.”**

To illustrate the correct treatment, consider the following example.

Suppose a company has **taxable income before depreciation of Rs. 100**, while the depreciation allowable under section 22 amounts to **Rs. 200**.

In such a situation, the depreciation deduction will first be adjusted against the available income of Rs. 100. As a result, the taxable income for the year will be reduced to **nil**. The remaining **Rs. 100** (being the portion of depreciation that could not be absorbed during the year) will not be treated as a **business loss**. Rather, it will be treated as **unabsorbed depreciation**, which may be carried forward and deducted against business income in subsequent tax years when such income becomes available.

It is important to distinguish this situation from a case where the company already has a **business loss before considering depreciation**.

For instance, if the business results before depreciation reflect a **loss of Rs. 100**, this amount represents a **business loss** for the purposes of the Ordinance. The treatment of such loss is governed by **section 57 of the Ordinance**, which provides that a loss under the head **“Income from Business”** may be carried forward and set off against income from business in subsequent tax years, subject to certain statutory conditions. One of the key limitations under section 57 is that **business losses may generally be carried forward for a maximum period of six tax years** immediately succeeding the tax year in which the loss was incurred.

In this scenario, therefore, the **operational loss of Rs. 100** would be treated as a **business loss under section 57**, while the depreciation allowance would retain its character as depreciation under **section 22**. To the extent such depreciation cannot be absorbed in the relevant year, it would continue to remain **unabsorbed depreciation** available for adjustment in future years.

Accordingly, the Ordinance maintains a clear distinction between **business losses** and **unabsorbed depreciation**, both in terms of their legal nature and their carry-forward rules. While **business losses are governed by section 57 and subject to the six-year carry-forward limitation**, the **unabsorbed portion of depreciation continues to be carried forward as depreciation allowance** until it is fully absorbed against future business income.

This distinction is important when forecasting future taxable positions, evaluating the utilization of carried-forward deductions, and planning the tax position of group entities over multiple years.

Please feel free to reach out should you wish to discuss how these rules may affect the projected tax position of your entities in the coming years.

Kind regards,  
[Your Name]

Your question is very valid from a technical perspective because the term **“unabsorbed depreciation”** is widely used in tax practice, yet it is important to understand whether the **Income Tax Ordinance, 2001** actually defines this term.

The position is that the Ordinance **does not expressly define the term “unabsorbed depreciation.”** Rather, the concept emerges from the mechanism of computing business income and allowing depreciation deductions under the relevant provisions of the law. In other words, the term is a **practical and interpretational expression** used by practitioners, tax authorities, and courts to describe depreciation that cannot be adjusted in the relevant tax year.

To understand this properly, the relevant provisions of the Ordinance must be read together.

First, **section 18 of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001** governs the computation of **income under the head “Income from Business.”** It provides that the income chargeable to tax under this head is the **profits and gains of a person’s business** for the tax year, computed in accordance with the provisions of the Ordinance.

In computing such income, taxpayers are entitled to claim various deductions that are specifically allowed under the law. One of the key deductions is **depreciation on depreciable assets**, which is governed by **section 22 of the Ordinance**.

Under **section 22(1)**, a person is allowed a **depreciation deduction for a tax year for any depreciable asset that is used in the person’s business during that year.** The amount of depreciation allowable is determined in accordance with the **rates and rules prescribed in Part I of the Third Schedule to the Ordinance**.

However, section 22 simply provides the **allowance of depreciation as a deduction**; it does not state that if depreciation exceeds income it should create a business loss. Instead, the legal framework assumes that depreciation is first applied against the available business income of the year.

Where the depreciation deduction **cannot be fully adjusted against the income of that year**, the unadjusted portion continues to retain its character as **depreciation allowance available for adjustment in future years**. In tax practice, this remaining amount is commonly referred to as **“unabsorbed depreciation.”**

The reason it is not treated as a **business loss** is because depreciation is a **statutory allowance linked to the capital asset base of the business**, rather than a loss arising from business operations.

A simple illustration may clarify the concept.

Assume that a company has **business income before depreciation of Rs. 100**, while the depreciation allowable under section 22 amounts to **Rs. 200**.

In this situation, the depreciation deduction will first be adjusted against the available income of Rs. 100. As a result, the taxable income for the year will be reduced to **nil**. The remaining **Rs. 100**, which represents depreciation that could not be absorbed in the current year, will not be treated as a business loss. Instead, it will continue as **depreciation allowance available for adjustment in subsequent tax years**. In professional and administrative practice, this amount is referred to as **unabsorbed depreciation**.

It is important to distinguish this from **business losses**, which are governed by **section 57 of the Ordinance**. Section 57 provides that where a taxpayer sustains a **loss under the head “Income from Business,”** such loss may be carried forward and set off against income from business in subsequent tax years, subject to certain conditions. One of the key limitations is that **business losses may generally be carried forward for a maximum period of six tax years** immediately following the year in which the loss was incurred.

Accordingly, the Ordinance recognizes two separate concepts:

• **Business losses**, which arise from operational results and are governed by **section 57** with a six-year carry-forward limitation.  
• **Depreciation allowance under section 22**, which may remain unadjusted in a particular year and continue to be available for deduction in subsequent years. This remaining portion is referred to in tax practice as **unabsorbed depreciation**.

Therefore, although the phrase **“unabsorbed depreciation”** is not explicitly defined in the Ordinance, it is a **recognized concept derived from the interaction of section 18 (business income computation), section 22 (depreciation allowance), and section 57 (carry forward of business losses)**. It represents the portion of depreciation that could not be adjusted in the relevant tax year and remains available for adjustment against future business income.

Understanding this distinction is particularly important when forecasting future taxable income, evaluating the utilization of carried-forward deductions, and ensuring that **business losses and depreciation allowances are not incorrectly merged in tax computations**.
