Below are the key observations and suggested improvements.

---

### 1. Missing Basic Contract Particulars
The opening clause leaves critical information blank.

The contract currently states that it is entered into **“as of ___ by and between Employer and Employee”** but the following are missing:

- Contract effective date  
- Employee full name  
- Employee CNIC  
- Designation / job title  

For legal clarity, this section should read more formally:

**Suggested wording**

> This Employment Contract (“Contract”) is made on ___ 2026 between **Averroes Learning Group**, having its office at 162/B-2, Block-3, PECHS, Karachi (hereinafter referred to as the “Employer”) and **Mr./Ms. _________**, CNIC No. ________, residing at ________ (hereinafter referred to as the “Employee”). fileciteturn0file0

Including CNIC and address helps enforce the agreement if any dispute arises.

---

### 2. Position Clause Should Be More Precise
Currently the contract states:

> “The Employee is hired as a ___.” fileciteturn0file0

The designation should be clearly defined, and you should also add reporting hierarchy.

**Improved clause**

> The Employee is appointed as **Homeroom Teacher / Teaching Assistant / [designation]** and shall report to the **Academic Coordinator / Principal** or any person designated by the Employer.

This avoids confusion regarding supervision.

---

### 3. Salary Clause – Add Payment Method and Deductions
The current clause only states salary and payment date. fileciteturn0file0

It should clarify:

- payment method
- statutory deductions
- tax implications

**Suggested improvement**

> The Employee shall receive a gross monthly salary of PKR ______. Salary shall be paid through bank transfer by the **10th day of the following month**, subject to deductions required under applicable laws including income tax, EOBI, or other statutory contributions, if applicable.

This protects the school from disputes regarding deductions.

---

### 4. Probation Clause Needs Confirmation Language
The probation clause is fine but missing confirmation terms.

**Suggested addition**

> Upon satisfactory completion of the probation period, the Employee’s employment shall be confirmed in writing by the Employer.

Without this, employees sometimes claim automatic confirmation.

---

### 5. Duties Clause Should Include Flexibility
The duties listed are detailed but slightly rigid. fileciteturn0file0

It is safer to include a broader operational clause.

**Suggested addition**

> The Employee shall perform all duties assigned by the Employer from time to time which are reasonably related to the Employee’s position and the operations of the school.

This prevents disputes over “that is not my job”.

---

### 6. Working Hours Clause Should Mention Overtime / Events
The clause currently mentions timings and occasional Saturdays. fileciteturn0file0

You should clarify that school events and meetings are part of normal duties.

**Improved wording**

> The Employee’s working hours shall be from 7:45 AM to 2:00 PM Monday to Thursday and until 1:30 PM on Friday. The Employee may also be required to attend staff meetings, training sessions, school functions, or parent meetings outside regular hours without additional compensation.

This is common in education sector contracts.

---

### 7. Termination Clause Should Cover Misconduct
Currently termination is only notice-based. fileciteturn0file0

It should also cover **immediate termination for misconduct**.

**Suggested clause**

> The Employer reserves the right to terminate employment without notice in cases of gross misconduct, breach of confidentiality, neglect of duties, or conduct detrimental to the reputation or safety of the school or students.

This is extremely important in school environments.

---

### 8. June & July Salary Clause Needs Clarification
This clause could cause disputes.

It currently states salary is payable only after completion of a full academic year. fileciteturn0file0

Two clarifications are needed:

- what happens if the employee resigns earlier
- what happens if employment ends during summer

**Suggested clarification**

> In case the Employee resigns or employment is terminated before completion of the academic year, no salary shall be payable for June and July.

---

### 9. Leave Policy Is Too Minimal
Seven paid leaves is fine but incomplete. fileciteturn0file0

You should clarify:

- sick leave
- unpaid leave
- leave accumulation

Example improvement:

> The Employee shall be entitled to **seven (7) paid casual leave days** per academic year. Sick leave may be granted at the discretion of the Employer upon submission of medical evidence.

---

### 10. Lateness Clause Is Legally Weak
The clause allows salary deduction for three late arrivals. fileciteturn0file0

However it should specify the time threshold.

**Suggested wording**

> An employee arriving more than **15 minutes late** will be considered late. Three instances of lateness in a month may result in one day’s salary deduction or leave adjustment.

Otherwise disputes may arise.

---

### 11. Add a Confidentiality Clause (Important)
Schools deal with sensitive student information.

Suggested clause:

> The Employee shall maintain strict confidentiality regarding student information, academic records, internal policies, and operational matters of the school during and after employment.

---

### 12. Add Governing Law Clause
This is a standard legal clause.

> This Contract shall be governed by and interpreted in accordance with the laws of the Islamic Republic of Pakistan.

---

### 13. Add Employee Handbook Reference
Schools usually operate through policies.

Suggested clause:

> The Employee agrees to comply with all school policies, code of conduct, safeguarding policies, and academic guidelines issued by the Employer from time to time.

---

### Final Professional Observation
The contract is operationally workable but **currently reads more like a policy document rather than a legal employment agreement**. With the improvements above, it will become clearer, more enforceable, and more professional.

When a person remains inside the **organizational chain of command**, the law tends to treat almost every payment as salary—even if the role temporarily expands or spans multiple companies in a group. Pakistani tax law focuses less on job titles and more on **whether the payment arises because of employment**.

These facts are critical.

### Why the income logically falls under “Salary”

Under **Section 12(2) of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001**, *salary* includes:

> any wages, remuneration, allowance or other amount received by an employee in respect of employment.

The phrase **“in respect of employment”** is deliberately broad. It covers not only basic salary but **any allowance, bonus, perquisite or additional remuneration arising because of the employment relationship**.

In your situation:

1. The assignment arose from an **internal Board-approved management decision**, not from an independent services contract.
2. You **remain under the organizational control of the Fauji Group management structure**.

4. The role is **temporary additional charge**, not a separate professional engagement.
5. There is **no independent billing arrangement or consultancy agreement**.

Because of these characteristics, the payment is **remuneration arising from employment**, which falls squarely within **Section 12**.

### Supporting jurisprudence and tax principle

Pakistani courts and appellate tribunals have repeatedly applied the **“employer-employee test”** to determine whether income should be taxed as salary or professional income. Key indicators considered include:

- **Control and supervision by the employer**
- **Integration into the organizational hierarchy**
- **Absence of independent commercial risk**
- **Payment structured as allowance or remuneration**

In several decisions of the **Appellate Tribunal Inland Revenue (ATIR)** dealing with directors’ remuneration and additional allowances paid to employees of group companies, the tribunals have held that **amounts received for performing duties within the employer’s organizational framework remain taxable under the head “Salary”, even where the duties are performed for another related entity**.

The underlying reasoning is straightforward:  
if the payment arises **because of employment**, it is salary.

### Practical withholding implication

Once classified as salary:

- The amount becomes part of **taxable salary under Section 12**.
- Withholding tax is required under **Section 149**.
- The amount should be reported in the **annual salary certificate and personal return**.

**Operational and Geological Drivers Affecting Output Sales Tax**

The decrease in output sales tax during the current period is primarily attributable to operational and geological factors affecting production levels, together with certain adjustments relating to previously paid sales tax.

From an operational perspective, United Energy Pakistan (“UEP”) operates a number of mature oil and gas fields, particularly within the Sindh province and the Badin block, which were acquired following the acquisition of British Petroleum’s Pakistani portfolio in 2011. As is typical in the upstream petroleum sector, mature fields progressively enter the **terminal decline phase** of their lifecycle. In petroleum engineering terms, this phase is characterized by a gradual and predictable reduction in hydrocarbon flow rates as reservoir pressure and natural deliverability diminish over time. Sector-wide analyses of Pakistan’s upstream industry similarly indicate that crude oil production has declined over the past decade largely due to depletion of mature reservoirs and limited replacement through new discoveries.

In the absence of **incremental producing streams or new discoveries**, such as new productive wells or additional exploration successes, the natural decline of mature reservoirs is not offset by new volumes. Consequently, the overall production baseline trends downward. This reduction in production volumes directly translates into a corresponding decline in taxable supplies, and therefore lower output sales tax reported in the monthly sales tax returns.

In addition to natural decline, production volumes may also be influenced by **production curtailment and dispatch constraints**, which are a recognized feature of the energy sector in Pakistan. Offtake levels for crude oil and gas can be affected by factors such as demand fluctuations, nominations by buyers, system or infrastructure limitations, and broader gas or LNG dispatch dynamics. Public sector reporting and industry disclosures have also acknowledged that gas curtailment and dispatch adjustments may materially affect the volumes lifted and invoiced by exploration and production companies, which in turn impacts the taxable value of supplies.

Furthermore, **pricing dynamics** also influence the taxable value of supplies. Even where production volumes decline only moderately, a reduction in realized prices — arising from movements in international benchmarks or adjustments under applicable gas pricing review mechanisms — reduces the value of taxable supplies. Since output sales tax is calculated on the value of supply, any reduction in realized price correspondingly lowers the output sales tax generated in the relevant period.

**Adjustment for Previously Paid Sales Tax**

Separately, the decrease in sales tax payments during the current period is also attributable to adjustments relating to sales tax that had been previously paid or advanced. In practice, upstream companies may remit sales tax in advance or pay excess amounts due to conservative estimates, timing differences, or subsequent reconciliations. Where such excess payments arise, the applicable provisions of the **Sales Tax Act, 1990** permit the taxpayer to claim refund or adjust such excess tax, provided the claim is made within the prescribed statutory timelines.

Accordingly, where UEP had previously remitted sales tax in advance or paid amounts in excess of the final liability, those amounts may be adjusted against the output tax liability of subsequent periods. In such cases, although the physical production and taxable supplies are duly reported in the sales tax returns, the **net sales tax payable for the period may appear reduced or even nil**, as the corresponding tax had effectively already been remitted to the government in earlier periods.

Accordingly, the scope of taxation was schedule-driven, and not definition-driven.

However, pursuant to the Finance Act, 2025, a fundamental structural shift has been introduced. The reliance on the Second Schedule has effectively been removed, and Section 3 has been aligned with a broader charging mechanism whereby all services are now taxable unless specifically falling within the negative list or otherwise exempt. In addition, the scope of “services” has been expanded to expressly include rights, obligations and other economic activities. Therefore, the current framework represents a transition from a “positive list” regime to a “negative list / universal taxability” regime.

In view of the above, the understanding that the scope of taxability remains unchanged does not appear to be consistent with the amended statutory scheme.

Secondly, with regard to the reliance on the Tribunal decision, it is important to appreciate that a decision which is under contest or capable of being challenged does not attain finality so as to become binding on the taxpayer in all circumstances. Thirdly, an important practical implication arises in relation to the manner of tax discharge. Any amount paid through the sales tax return is treated as an admitted liability under the law. Such payments are not regarded as being made “under protest,” and therefore, even if the taxpayer ultimately succeeds in litigation, recovery of such amounts may not be straightforward. This creates a significant commercial and legal exposure if a position is adopted in returns without due evaluation.

Further, from a compliance perspective, the law requires that invoices clearly specify the nature of service along with the relevant tariff heading / classification. At the same time, it is important to note that the **definition of “franchise” itself has not undergone any material change**. However, the **legal and charging context within which such definition operates has significantly evolved**, due to:

- the shift from a **positive list to a universal taxability regime**, and  
- the **expanded definition of service capturing rights and economic arrangements**.

Accordingly, reliance on earlier classification (including treatment as “franchise”) without revisiting the broader charging provision and amended definition of service may not be aligned with the current statutory framework.

---

### Why this works (strategically)

This does three subtle but powerful things:

- It shifts debate from **“is it franchise or not?” → to “even if not franchise, it is still a taxable service via rights”**
- It aligns Sindh with **Punjab-style economic substance taxation**
- It weakens PQA’s comfort zone (Tribunal decision) by showing **law has evolved at definitional level, not just procedural**

In simple terms: earlier law taxed *named services*; now it taxes *economic value itself*.

And once “rights” enter the arena, port concessions, terminal access, berthing priority, etc.—all start looking less like labels and more like taxable economic privileges.

Dear Muhammad Ali,  

We refer to the applicability of withholding tax on dividends in light of the Double Tax Treaty between the Sultanate of Oman and the Islamic Republic of Pakistan. The treaty provides specific guidance on the taxation of dividends paid by a company resident in Pakistan to a recipient resident in Oman, with differentiated rates depending upon the nature of the recipient and its shareholding in the Pakistani company.  

Under the treaty provisions, dividends paid by a Pakistani resident company to a company resident in Oman are taxable in Pakistan at a reduced rate of 10%, provided that the recipient qualifies as a “company” and holds at least 10% of the share capital of the Pakistani company. In all other cases, the applicable treaty rate is 12.5%.  

The term “company” for treaty purposes generally includes any body corporate or any entity treated as a body corporate for tax purposes. In substance, a body corporate refers to an entity having a separate legal personality, established through law or incorporation, with the capacity to own assets, enter into contracts, and carry on business independently of its members or the State.  

Based on a review of publicly available information, the Oman Investment Authority (OIA) appears to meet the above criteria. It has been established through a Royal Decree in Oman, which confers upon it a distinct legal identity separate from the government. Furthermore, it operates independently, manages investments, enters into contractual arrangements, and undertakes commercial activities in its own name. From a tax perspective as well, its structure and governance framework are consistent with entities that are treated as corporate bodies.  

Accordingly, in our view, OIA should qualify as a “company” for the purposes of the treaty. Therefore, dividends paid by a Pakistani resident company to OIA may be subject to withholding tax at the reduced rate of 10%, provided the minimum shareholding threshold of 10% is satisfied.  

It is, however, pertinent to highlight that the process of formally replacing the State General Reserve Fund (SGRF) with the Oman Investment Authority (OIA) in the treaty/protocol is currently underway. Once this substitution is officially notified, OIA would be entitled to the more beneficial rate of 5% on gross dividends as specifically provided for SGRF. Until such time, the concessional 5% rate would not be available, and the standard treaty rates (i.e., 10% / 12.5%) would continue to apply.

Dear Zeeshan,

I have carefully revisited the PwC advice dated 29 January 2026 . Broadly, their technical analysis aligns with section 153 of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001; however, two areas require clearer articulation before KE proceeds with accepting bifurcation of invoices.

Firstly, the treatment of “goods” must be strictly confined to medicines supplied through OMI’s pharmacy in the true commercial sense. The opinion refers specifically to pharmacy sales, which is an important qualifier. The 5% withholding under section 153(1)(a) can only be supported where medicines are sold as standalone, off-the-shelf trading goods — separately identifiable, separately priced, and capable of independent sale through the pharmacy counter. A clear distinction must be maintained between such pharmacy sales and medicines administered during hospitalization as part of medical treatment. Medicines supplied in the course of inpatient care form an integral part of the healthcare service package. Even if itemised on the invoice, they remain embedded in the service component and should not automatically be carved out and treated as “goods.” Therefore, bifurcation should only be accepted where the pharmacy component genuinely represents an independent trading transaction. It would not be appropriate to treat all medicine line items as goods without examining the context of supply.

Secondly, the reimbursement discussion in the advice requires cautious application from KE’s standpoint. In law, reimbursement exists only where an expense is incurred specifically on behalf of KE, supported by third-party documentation, passed through at actual cost, and without any embedded profit element. Where OMI allocates doctors’ fees or other operational costs from its general revenue pool and includes such charges in the invoice, this does not qualify as reimbursement in the strict legal sense. Allocation of internal or pooled costs is not equivalent to a pass-through expense incurred on KE’s behalf. Unless there is a specific arrangement under which OMI incurs a cost exclusively for KE and merely recovers it without markup, such amounts remain consideration for services and would attract withholding accordingly. From a compliance perspective, reimbursement treatment should therefore not be assumed merely on the basis of invoice description.

Subject to these clarifications, the remaining analysis in the opinion appears technically sound. **Subject:** Tax Implications of Cross-Border Employment – Summary of Discussion and Way Forward  

Dear [Client Name],  

We refer to our recent discussion regarding the tax implications arising from the deployment of certain employees from the Pakistan branch to overseas operations (Mukistan), including the pattern of working days abroad and periodic return to Pakistan in line with operational requirements and industry practices (i.e., field and non-field rotations, leave cycles, etc.).  

Based on the understanding shared during the meeting, our analysis under the **Income Tax Ordinance, 2001** is summarised below for your consideration:  

---

### **1. Fundamental Principle – Taxation of Employment Income**  
Under Pakistani tax law, salary income is primarily taxed on the basis of **where employment is exercised** (Section 12 read with source rules). Accordingly:  

- Salary attributable to employment exercised **outside Pakistan** is generally treated as **foreign source income**.  
- However, the **taxability in Pakistan depends critically on the individual’s residential status** for the relevant tax year (July to June), as determined under **Section 82** of the Ordinance.  

---

### **2. Determination of Residential Status (Section 82)**  
Each employee must be evaluated individually to determine whether they qualify as:  

- **Resident Individual** – broadly, presence in Pakistan for **183 days or more** during the tax year; or  
- **Non-Resident Individual** – where the above threshold is not met.  

This determination is a **question of fact** and forms the foundation for taxability analysis.  

---

### **3. Tax Treatment – Scenario Analysis**

#### **Scenario A: Resident Individual**

If an individual qualifies as a **resident**, then:  

- Under **Section 11 (read with global income concept)**, **worldwide income** becomes taxable in Pakistan.  
- Accordingly, foreign employment income (i.e., salary earned in Mukistan) will be taxable in Pakistan **unless specifically exempt**.  

**Possible Relief – Foreign Tax Credit / Exemption:**  
- Where such foreign salary has been **subject to tax in the foreign jurisdiction**, relief may be available under:  
  - **Section 103 (Foreign Tax Credit)**; or  
  - Applicable **Double Tax Treaty**, if any.  

- However, **if no tax has been paid abroad**, the **entire salary would be taxable in Pakistan**.  

**Important Clarification (Return before June):**  
During the discussion, it was noted that employees frequently travel back and forth between Pakistan and Mukistan. In such cases:  

- The specific exemption available to individuals who **leave Pakistan for employment abroad and remain outside Pakistan for the entire remainder of the tax year (i.e., do not return before June)** would **not be available**.  
- This is because the condition of **continuous absence** is not met due to rotational travel.  

---

#### **Scenario B: Non-Resident Individual**

If an individual qualifies as a **non-resident**, then:  

- Under **Section 11 read with Section 101**, only **Pakistan-source income** is taxable in Pakistan.  
- Salary earned for employment **exercised outside Pakistan** would generally **not be taxable in Pakistan**, even if paid from Pakistan.  

Given your operational model:  

- Where employment duties are substantively performed outside Pakistan, such income would likely **not fall within Pakistan-source income** for a non-resident individual.  
- Accordingly, **no tax exposure should arise in Pakistan on such foreign employment income**.  

---

### **4. Decision Framework (Simplified)**  

To facilitate internal assessment, the position may be viewed through the following decision logic:  

**Step 1 – Determine Residential Status**  
- If **Resident → go to Step 2**  
- If **Non-Resident → foreign salary not taxable in Pakistan**  

**Step 2 – For Resident Individuals**  
- Has foreign salary been **taxed abroad?**  
  - **Yes → Relief available (FTC / Treaty), subject to conditions**  
  - **No → Fully taxable in Pakistan**  

**Additional Consideration:**  
- Frequent travel (back-and-forth) → **No exemption for continuous foreign employment**  

---

### **5. Practical Considerations and Way Forward**

Based on the above, the tax outcome can be managed through two broad approaches:  

1. **Foreign Tax Alignment (for Residents):**  
   - Ensuring that employment income is **subject to tax in the foreign jurisdiction**, thereby enabling **foreign tax credit relief in Pakistan**.  

2. **Non-Resident Status Planning:**  
   - Evaluating whether employees can **qualify as non-residents under Section 82**, based on actual presence patterns.  
   - This may require a **careful cost-benefit analysis**, considering both tax and operational implications.  

---

### **6. Concluding Remarks**

In summary, the taxability of such cross-border employment arrangements is highly dependent on **residential status and actual place of employment exercise**, with significant implications arising from travel patterns and foreign tax exposure.  

We recommend conducting an **employee-wise analysis** to determine:  
- Days of presence in Pakistan;  
- Nature and location of employment duties;  
- Foreign tax position (if any);  

This will enable a **defensible and tax-efficient structuring** aligned with the Ordinance.

Under Pakistani tax law, salary income is generally taxed based on the **place where employment is exercised**, in terms of **Section 12 read with Section 101 of the Ordinance**. Therefore, where employment duties are performed outside Pakistan, the resulting income is treated as **foreign source income**.  

However, the ultimate taxability in Pakistan depends on whether the individual is classified as a **resident or non-resident**, and whether specific exemption conditions are met.

Where an individual qualifies as a **resident person**, Pakistan follows a **global income taxation principle** under **Section 11**, whereby worldwide income, including foreign employment income, is generally taxable in Pakistan.

- employment is exercised outside Pakistan; and  
- the corresponding salary income has been **subjected to tax in the foreign jurisdiction**,  

such income is **not chargeable to tax in Pakistan**. This is not merely a foreign tax credit mechanism under Section 103, but rather operates as a **substantive exemption**, provided the condition of taxability abroad is satisfied.  

Conversely, where no tax has been discharged in the foreign jurisdiction, the exemption would not be available, and the **entire foreign employment income would become taxable in Pakistan**.

By way of background, while the MYT for the relevant control period was notified by the National Electric Power Regulatory Authority (“NEPRA”) in July 2025, subsequent review and reconsideration proceedings resulted in a substantial downward revision of the tariff. Given the material financial implications of such revisions, the Company has exercised its lawful remedies before the appropriate forums.

## **1. ILLEGAL ASSUMPTION OF JURISDICTION – SECTIONS 177, 214C AND CONSEQUENT INVALIDITY OF SECTION 122 PROCEEDINGS**

At the very outset, it is respectfully submitted that the entire proceedings are fundamentally vitiated due to lack of lawful jurisdiction. The scheme of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001 clearly envisages that selection of a taxpayer for audit is governed by **section 214C**, which mandates selection through computer balloting or other prescribed transparent mechanisms.

Section 177, which empowers the Commissioner to conduct audit, cannot be read in isolation. Rather, it must be harmoniously construed with section 214C, which regulates the manner and conditions under which such power may be exercised. Any audit conducted outside this statutory framework constitutes an assumption of jurisdiction without lawful authority.

In the present case, it is an admitted position that the Appellant’s case was not selected through the prescribed balloting process. Consequently, the initiation of audit proceedings under section 177 was inherently unlawful. Since the subsequent amendment under section 122 is entirely founded upon such audit, the illegality strikes at the root of the proceedings.

It is a settled principle that **jurisdictional defects are not curable irregularities**. Once the foundation is illegal, the superstructure cannot survive. This principle is embedded within the scheme of tax jurisprudence, where strict adherence to statutory conditions is mandatory.

Further, section 122 empowers amendment of assessment only where valid proceedings exist. Where the underlying audit itself is void, any consequential amendment lacks legal basis.

Accordingly, the impugned order deserves to be annulled in limine.

## **2. DISALLOWANCE OF WRITE-OFF OF ASSETS – SECTIONS 20 AND 21**

The disallowance of write-off of assets reflects a misapplication of the fundamental charging and deduction provisions of the Ordinance.

Section 20 provides that **any expenditure or loss incurred wholly and exclusively for the purposes of business shall be deductible**, except to the extent specifically disallowed under section 21. The scheme of the law, therefore, is permissive in nature, with disallowances being strictly construed.

The write-off of assets represents a crystallized business loss arising from obsolescence or irrecoverability. It is neither a capital outlay nor a fictitious entry; rather, it reflects the true financial position of the business.

The Ordinance does not contain any provision disallowing such write-offs. In absence of a specific prohibition under section 21, the deduction must be allowed.

It is further submitted that tax authorities cannot question commercial expediency unless mala fide or non-business purpose is established. This principle flows from the interpretation of section 20 and has been consistently upheld in jurisprudence.

In the present case, no material has been brought on record to establish that the write-off was not genuine or not incurred in the course of business. Therefore, the disallowance is contrary to the scheme of the Ordinance.

---

## **3. ADDITION ON ACCOUNT OF DEPOSITS WRITTEN OFF – CONCEPT OF REAL INCOME (SECTION 4 READ WITH SECTION 18)**

The addition made on account of deposits written off is legally unsustainable as it disregards the fundamental principle that **tax is chargeable only on real income under section 4 of the Ordinance**.

Section 18 defines business income as income derived from business activities. A write-off of deposits does not generate income; rather, it represents a diminution of assets.

The Department has failed to identify any charging provision under which such amount could be brought to tax. In absence of a charging section, no tax can be imposed.

Further, even under section 39 (Income from Other Sources), the essential requirement is the existence of a **positive inflow or benefit**. A write-off, by its very nature, is a loss event and cannot be treated as income.

The settled doctrine of “real income” mandates that hypothetical or notional amounts cannot be subjected to tax. Therefore, the addition lacks both statutory basis and conceptual validity.

---

## **4. DISALLOWANCE UNDER SECTION 21(c) – CASH PAYMENTS (SUBSTANCE OVER FORM)**

The disallowance under section 21(c) has been made in a mechanical manner without appreciating the legislative intent of the provision.

Section 21(c) is a **restrictive provision**, and therefore must be strictly construed. It does not render all cash payments inadmissible; rather, it applies subject to conditions, thresholds, and factual context.

The provision aims to curb non-transparent transactions, not to penalize genuine business expenditures. Where payments are:

- duly recorded in books,  
- made for business purposes, and  
- not disputed in terms of genuineness,  

then disallowance merely due to mode of payment defeats the purpose of taxation based on real income.

Further, the commercial realities of the Appellant’s business necessitated certain cash payments, particularly in operational contexts where banking channels were not feasible.

It is also relevant that section 21(c) does not override section 20; rather, both must be read harmoniously. Where the expenditure satisfies the test of section 20 and no abuse is demonstrated, disallowance is unwarranted.

## **5. ADDITION ON DISPOSAL OF ASSETS – MISAPPLICATION OF DEPRECIATION REGIME (SECTIONS 22 AND 23)**

The addition on account of gain on disposal of assets has been made without following the statutory framework governing depreciable assets.

Sections 22 and 23 lay down a complete mechanism for depreciation and treatment of disposal of assets. The concept of “written down value” is central to this regime.

Any gain or loss on disposal must be computed strictly in accordance with these provisions. The Department has failed to demonstrate that such statutory mechanism was followed.

Instead, an arbitrary addition has been made without reconciling:

- tax written down value,  
- disposal consideration, and  
- accumulated depreciation.  

Such an approach is contrary to the scheme of the Ordinance and renders the addition unsustainable.

## **6. DISALLOWANCE OF RENTAL EXPENDITURE – APPLICATION OF SECTION 20**

The rental expenditure incurred by the Appellant is a routine business expense and falls squarely within the ambit of section 20.

Once it is established that the expenditure has been incurred:

- wholly and exclusively for business, and  
- supported by documentary evidence,  

the same is allowable unless specifically disallowed under section 21.

The Department has not identified any specific violation under section 21. The disallowance appears to be based solely on mode of payment, which, as submitted earlier, is insufficient to deny deduction in absence of any adverse finding on genuineness.

Accordingly, the disallowance is contrary to the statutory framework.

---

## **7. DISALLOWANCE OF INITIAL ALLOWANCE – SECTION 23**

Section 23 provides for initial allowance on eligible depreciable assets. The entitlement depends upon:

- nature of asset,  
- use in business, and  
- compliance with conditions specified in law.  

The electrical fittings in question form part of the business infrastructure and qualify as depreciable assets.

The denial of initial allowance reflects an incorrect interpretation of section 23 and ignores the functional use of the assets in the Appellant’s business.

---

## **8. ADDITION UNDER SECTION 109 READ WITH SECTION 39 – BURDEN OF PROOF AND MISCHARACTERIZATION**

The addition under section 109 represents a significant misapplication of law.

Section 109 deals with **unexplained income**, and its invocation requires:

1. existence of an unexplained amount, and  
2. failure of the taxpayer to provide a satisfactory explanation.  

In the present case, the Appellant has provided complete explanation regarding stock transfer to GAM Corporation, supported by accounting records and documentation.

Once such explanation is furnished, the burden shifts to the Department to disprove it with evidence. Mere disbelief or suspicion is insufficient.

Further, the treatment of such transaction under section 39 (Income from Other Sources) is legally flawed. A business transaction cannot be recharacterized as unexplained income in absence of any defect in documentation.

The addition, therefore, violates both **burden of proof principles** and **statutory framework**.

---

## **9. DOUBLE TAXATION – MISAPPLICATION OF SECTION 113**

The computation of tax by simultaneously applying:

- minimum tax under section 113, and  
- normal tax under section 4  

is contrary to the scheme of the Ordinance.

Section 113 operates as a **minimum tax mechanism**, ensuring a floor for taxation where normal tax liability falls below a specified threshold. It is not intended to operate cumulatively.

The structure of the provision clearly indicates that the taxpayer is liable to pay **either minimum tax or normal tax, whichever is higher**, but not both.

The simultaneous application results in double taxation on the same income base, which is impermissible unless expressly provided by law.

The failure of the learned CIR(A) to adjudicate this issue further aggravates the illegality.

---

## **10. NON-ADJUSTMENT OF DEPRECIATION – SET-OFF MECHANISM (SECTIONS 22, 56, 57, 67)**

The issue relating to non-adjustment of depreciation has not been properly appreciated.

Depreciation forms part of business deductions under section 22 and contributes to determination of taxable income under the head “Income from Business.”

The Ordinance provides a comprehensive framework for **set-off and carry forward of losses** under sections 56 to 58 and section 67.

The denial of adjustment against income from other sources disregards this integrated scheme and results in artificial inflation of taxable income.

# **REFINED GROUNDS OF APPEAL (PARAGRAPH FORM – CONCISE)**

---

### **Ground No. 1 – Non-Speaking Order**

The impugned order is non-speaking and has been passed without proper application of mind. The learned CIR(A) has failed to consider and adjudicate upon the submissions and evidence placed on record. Such an order is violative of section 129 of the Ordinance and the principles of natural justice, including Article 10A of the Constitution, and is liable to be set aside.

---

### **Ground No. 2 – Invalid Jurisdiction under Section 122(5A)**

The learned officer has wrongly assumed jurisdiction under section 122(5A) without identifying any specific error in the original assessment or demonstrating that it was erroneous and prejudicial to the interest of revenue. The proceedings are based on vague allegations and amount to a fishing inquiry, which is beyond the scope of section 122(5A) and renders the proceedings void ab initio.

---

### **Ground No. 3 – Violation of Natural Justice**

The impugned order has been passed without affording a reasonable opportunity of being heard to the appellant. The appellant’s request for extension was not duly considered and the proceedings were concluded in an arbitrary manner. Such action is in clear violation of settled principles of natural justice and the order is therefore unsustainable.

---

### **Ground No. 4 – Profit on Debt – Business Income under Section 18**

The learned officer has erred in treating profit on debt as income from other sources under section 39, without appreciating that such income arises from mandatory security accounts maintained under project financing arrangements. The funds are not surplus but contractually restricted and the income is incidental to business operations. Accordingly, the same is chargeable under section 18 as business income.

---

### **Ground No. 5 – Misapplication of Section 39**

Section 39 is a residuary provision and can only be invoked where income does not fall under any specific head. In the present case, the income has a direct nexus with business operations and therefore cannot be brought under section 39. The impugned treatment is legally untenable.

---

### **Ground No. 6 – Interest on SSGCL Receivable**

The learned officer has failed to appreciate that the interest on receivable from SSGCL arises under the LNG Services Agreement and represents an accretion to the same contractual receipt. As per settled legal principles, such accretion partakes the character of the original receipt and forms part of exempt income under Clause 141 of the Second Schedule.

---

### **Ground No. 7 – Without Prejudice (Section 40)**

Without prejudice, even if the impugned income is assessed under section 39, the learned officer has erred in not allowing the corresponding expenses incurred for earning such income. In terms of section 40, such expenses are allowable and must be duly considered.

---

### **Ground No. 8 – General**

The appellant craves leave to add, amend, alter, or withdraw any of the above grounds at the time of hearing.

---

### **Grounds No. 1 to 4 – Jurisdictional Defects, Violation of Natural Justice & Invalid Assumption of Jurisdiction under Section 122(5A)**

At the outset, it is respectfully submitted that the impugned order passed under section 122(4) read with section 122(5A) of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001 is bad in law and on facts, having been issued without lawful jurisdiction and in violation of the mandatory conditions prescribed under the Ordinance. In the absence of any specific defect identified in the assessment or any independent inquiry conducted, the entire proceedings amount to a fishing and roving exercise, impermissible under the law and contrary to the settled legal position that amendment proceedings cannot be used as a substitute for audit.

The appellant had duly sought an extension of time vide letter dated February 23, 2026; however, no decision on such request was communicated and the order was passed hastily, thereby violating the principles of natural justice and the appellant’s fundamental right to due process. It is a settled principle that any order passed in breach of audi alteram partem is void ab initio.

The learned ACIR has also failed to pass a speaking order as required under section 129 of the Ordinance. The impugned order does not deal with the appellant’s submissions, nor does it provide any reasoning or application of mind on the issues raised. Such a cryptic and non-speaking order is liable to be struck down on this ground alone.

It is, therefore, respectfully prayed that the amendment proceedings initiated under section 122(5A) and the consequential order passed thereunder be declared illegal, without jurisdiction and void ab initio, and the original deemed assessment under section 120 be restored.

---

### **Ground No. 5 – Profit on Debt from Mandatory Project Accounts is Business Income under Section 18**

The learned ACIR has erred in law and on facts in treating the profit on debt earned on bank deposits amounting to Rs. 149,676,733 as “income from other sources” under section 39 of the Ordinance. The characterization is fundamentally flawed as it fails to appreciate the true nature, source and nexus of such income with the appellant’s core business operations.

It is respectfully submitted that the appellant operates an LNG terminal under a highly structured project financing arrangement involving international lenders. Under the terms of the financing agreements, the appellant is mandatorily required to maintain designated security and reserve accounts, wherein funds representing loan disbursements, project revenues and operational balances are held. These accounts are not discretionary investment vehicles; rather, they are integral to the project financing structure and are maintained under strict contractual obligations, with restricted utilization and predefined payment waterfalls.

The profit on debt arises automatically and incidentally on balances maintained in such mandatory accounts. It is not the result of any independent investment decision or deployment of surplus funds. The earning of such profit is a contractual consequence of maintaining project accounts, without any discretion available to the appellant. Accordingly, such income is intrinsically linked to, and arises in the course of, the appellant’s business operations.

In terms of section 18 of the Ordinance, all income arising from or incidental to the carrying on of business is chargeable as business income. Section 39, being a residuary provision, applies only where income does not fall under any specific head. Where income is inextricably connected with business operations, it cannot be artificially segregated and brought under section 39.

In view of the above, the profit on debt constitutes business income and is chargeable under section 18. The impugned treatment under section 39 is therefore legally unsustainable and liable to be set aside.

Without prejudice to the above, even if the said income is assumed, arguendo, to fall under section 39, the learned ACIR has erred in failing to allow the corresponding expenses incurred wholly and exclusively for earning such income, as mandated under section 40 of the Ordinance. The impugned order, therefore, suffers from a fundamental legal defect as it taxes gross income without permitting legitimate deductions, which is contrary to the scheme of taxation under the Ordinance.

---

The learned ACIR has further failed to appreciate that the funds maintained in the bank accounts do not represent surplus or idle funds available for investment; rather, these are project-specific balances maintained under lender covenants and financing arrangements. The earning of profit thereon is merely incidental and cannot be regarded as a separate source of income independent of business operations. The impugned treatment is therefore based on an incorrect assumption of facts and is liable to be vacated.

Where the reasons are well-documented, unavoidable, and demonstrate bona fide conduct, the chances of approval are generally reasonable; however, weak or procedural delays are typically not entertained favorably.

From a jurisdictional perspective, there has been a notable shift in the approval mechanism. Previously, the Commissioner Inland Revenue was empowered to condone delays up to one year, which was subsequently enhanced to three years. Currently, the effective threshold stands at two years, beyond which the matter falls outside the Commissioner’s authority and requires approval from the Federal Board of Revenue. Based on our understanding of your case, the period involved appears to exceed this threshold, and accordingly, the application is likely to be placed before the Board, where the scrutiny tends to be more stringent and formalized.

Therefore, it would be necessary to justify not only the supplier’s delay but also the subsequent time taken by your organization in identifying and rectifying the issue. Any gap attributable to internal oversight or delayed action on your part may weaken the overall position, as condonation is not ordinarily granted for delays arising from internal inefficiencies. پندرہ میں ان کو کہا ہے کہ آپ گراؤنڈز کو بھی ریوزٹ کریں اور اس کو کریں پراپر کریں تاکہ مور افیکٹیو وے میں آپ جنے ٹربیونل میں اپیل لڑ سکیں اب جو لائر کا پوائنٹ آف ویو یہ ہے کہ اپریل میں اس کی ہیرنگ فکس ہوگی اور وہ کہہ رہے ہیں کہ ایس پر دیئر ریڈنگ کہ یہ ریمانڈ پیک ہو جائے گا ہم نے اس کو پلیڈ کیے کہ آپ تھوڑا سا اس پہ تھوڑا سا اور ایففرٹ پٹن کر کے کوشش کریں کہ ڈلیٹ ہو انسٹیٹ آف ریمانڈ پہ تو وہ اس نے Dear [Client Name],  

We refer to our earlier advice wherein we had evaluated the tax implications of the initially proposed structure. Subsequently, we have reviewed the revised transaction model shared by you, along with the legal opinion obtained from MTC covering the alternative scenarios. Based on a combined reading of the revised commercial arrangement and the legal position articulated therein, we set out below our considered views from a Pakistan income tax perspective.

At the outset, it is pertinent to note that the revised model represents a fundamental shift in the underlying structure, particularly with the introduction of an independent third-party intermediary in place of the earlier related-party arrangement. From a technical standpoint, this change materially alters the tax profile of the transaction. In particular, the concerns arising under the transfer pricing framework, as envisaged under section 108 of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001, would no longer be directly applicable in the absence of an associated enterprise relationship. Similarly, considerations relating to controlled foreign company provisions under section 109A would not arise where the intermediary entity is not owned or controlled by a Pakistani resident. In this respect, the revised model is inherently more aligned with a conventional export distribution structure and, therefore, carries a comparatively lower degree of regulatory sensitivity.

That said, it would be important to appreciate that, in practice, the tax authorities in Pakistan tend to evaluate such arrangements not only on their legal form but also on their underlying commercial substance. In particular, where there is a visible divergence between the economic value generated within Pakistan and the margins retained offshore, the authorities may seek to examine whether the pricing of exports appropriately reflects the functions performed and risks assumed by the respective parties. Accordingly, even in the absence of a related-party relationship, the pricing mechanism may still be subject to scrutiny from a broader commercial rationality perspective.

In this context, the sustainability of the revised structure would largely depend upon the extent to which the intermediary entity is able to demonstrate a genuine and independent commercial role within the supply chain. This would typically entail evidence that the intermediary is responsible for key functions such as market development, customer engagement, negotiation of sales, assumption of credit and inventory risks (where applicable), and compliance with regulatory requirements in the destination markets. Where such attributes are demonstrably present, the allocation of margins outside Pakistan would generally be more defensible. Conversely, if the intermediary’s role is limited in substance and the core commercial decisions continue to be undertaken by the Pakistan entity, there may be a basis for the tax authorities to question the arrangement, including the possibility of recharacterizing the transaction in line with its economic reality.

We further note that, notwithstanding the above considerations, the tax position in Pakistan would, in any event, continue to be influenced by the applicable withholding tax regime on export proceeds. As such, the overall tax incidence for the Pakistan entity is likely to remain linked to turnover, which provides a degree of stability to the tax cost irrespective of the ultimate profit distribution across jurisdictions.

Having considered the legal opinion provided by MTC, particularly in relation to Scenario 1, we are broadly aligned with the view that the proposed structure may be sustained where it reflects a bona fide third-party commercial arrangement. However, from a tax risk management perspective, it would be prudent to ensure that the contractual framework, pricing methodology, and operational conduct are consistently aligned and adequately documented. This would include clearly articulated agreements, contemporaneous support for pricing decisions, and demonstrable evidence of the intermediary’s independent role.

On an overall assessment, the revised model appears to be more robust and commercially defensible as compared to the earlier proposed structure. Nevertheless, its effectiveness from a tax standpoint would ultimately depend on the manner in which it is implemented and substantiated in practice. We would therefore recommend that appropriate attention is given to aligning the legal documentation with the actual conduct of the parties, so as to mitigate any potential exposure during assessment proceedings.

We would be pleased to discuss the above in further detail and assist, where required, in reviewing the underlying agreements or supporting documentation prior to implementation.

Subsequently, we have reviewed the revised model shared by you, along with the legal opinion obtained from MTC covering the two proposed scenarios. Based on a holistic review of the evolving structure, read together with the legal position articulated by your counsel, our consolidated views from a Pakistan income tax perspective are set out below.

---

### **Scenario 1 – Export through UAE Subsidiary (Related Party Structure)**  

Under this scenario, the Pakistan entity exports goods to its UAE-based subsidiary, which in turn undertakes onward sales to third-party customers. This structure, as also highlighted in our earlier advice, gives rise to direct implications under the transfer pricing framework prescribed under section 108 of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001, as the transactions are undertaken between associated enterprises.

In such cases, the primary focus of the tax authorities typically revolves around whether the pricing of exports appropriately reflects arm’s length principles, particularly in circumstances where a portion of the overall supply chain margin is retained outside Pakistan. Practically, where the Pakistan entity undertakes core functions such as manufacturing, assumes key operational risks, and retains control over commercial decision-making, the authorities may expect a commensurate share of profits to be recognized within Pakistan. Any deviation from this position, especially in the form of relatively lower export pricing to the related party, may trigger adjustments under section 108.

In addition to transfer pricing considerations, the structure also carries exposure under controlled foreign company provisions as contained in section 109A of the Ordinance, whereby undistributed profits of a low-taxed foreign subsidiary may be attributed to the resident parent, subject to prescribed thresholds and conditions. While the applicability of such provisions would depend on the factual matrix, including the nature of income and level of taxation in the foreign jurisdiction, the existence of such exposure remains an inherent feature of the structure.

We note that the legal opinion provided by MTC broadly aligns with the above considerations and acknowledges the potential sensitivities associated with a related-party routing structure. In particular, the emphasis on regulatory compliance, including State Bank of Pakistan requirements governing export proceeds and foreign exchange flows, further underscores that such arrangements are subject not only to tax scrutiny but also to broader regulatory oversight.

Overall, while the structure may be technically implementable, it carries a relatively higher degree of tax and regulatory exposure, primarily driven by transfer pricing adjustments, potential CFC implications, and the need to substantiate the commercial rationale of margin allocation across jurisdictions.

---

### **Scenario 2 – Export to Independent Third-Party Intermediary**  

Under the revised model, as currently understood, the Pakistan entity exports goods to an independent third-party intermediary, which subsequently undertakes onward sales in international markets. This represents a fundamental shift from the earlier related-party structure and materially alters the tax profile of the arrangement.

In the absence of an associated enterprise relationship, the specific provisions relating to transfer pricing under section 108 would not be directly applicable. Similarly, the considerations arising under section 109A relating to controlled foreign companies would also not arise. Consequently, the structural exposures that were inherent in Scenario 1 stand largely mitigated under this arrangement.

However, it is important to note that the absence of a related-party relationship does not, in itself, preclude scrutiny by the tax authorities. In practice, the authorities may still evaluate whether the pricing of exports reflects commercial reality, particularly in cases where significant margins are realized by the intermediary. In this regard, the emphasis shifts from formal transfer pricing compliance to a broader assessment of commercial substance and genuineness of the third-party arrangement.

In line with the observations made in the legal opinion by MTC, it becomes critical that the intermediary qualifies as a bona fide independent party with adequate commercial capacity. This would typically require that the intermediary demonstrates sufficient financial standing, operational capability, and an independent business rationale for its role within the supply chain. The intermediary should ideally be engaged in substantive functions such as market development, customer acquisition, negotiation of sales, and assumption of commercial risks, rather than merely acting as a pass-through entity.

Accordingly, it would be important to ensure that the arrangement is supported by appropriate documentation evidencing the intermediary’s independence, including contractual agreements, financial credentials, and operational involvement in the transaction flow. From a practical standpoint, the robustness of this structure would largely depend on whether the intermediary’s role can withstand scrutiny as a genuine commercial participant in the overall business model.

From a Pakistan tax perspective, the export proceeds arising from such transactions would continue to be subject to the applicable withholding tax regime, including provisions relating to export proceeds under the Ordinance. As such, the tax position of the Pakistan entity would, to a large extent, remain linked to turnover, thereby providing a relatively stable tax outcome irrespective of the distribution of profits across jurisdictions.

---

### **Conclusion**  

On an overall assessment, Scenario 2 appears to be comparatively more robust and defensible from a Pakistan income tax perspective, primarily due to the absence of related-party exposures and the resulting mitigation of transfer pricing and CFC-related risks. However, its sustainability is contingent upon the ability to demonstrate that the intermediary operates as a genuine independent entity with real commercial substance.

Scenario 1, while technically feasible, carries relatively higher exposure owing to the inherent sensitivities associated with related-party transactions, including transfer pricing adjustments, potential attribution of foreign profits, and increased regulatory scrutiny.

In light of the above, we would recommend that, if the revised model under Scenario 2 is pursued, particular emphasis should be placed on ensuring alignment between contractual terms and actual conduct, along with maintaining adequate supporting documentation to substantiate the commercial rationale of the arrangement.

We would be pleased to discuss the above further or assist in reviewing the underlying agreements and implementation framework to ensure that the proposed structure remains robust from both a tax and regulatory perspective.

This version does a few important things (which are critical in real client communication):

- Shows **continuity of discussion** (PwC → revised model → legal opinion)  
- Clearly defines **what input is required**  
- Pushes for **comparative + practical advice** (not just theoretical)  
- Keeps tone professional but natural (not overly legalistic)

- Make it **more assertive (partner-level tone)**, or  
- Slightly **shorten it for quick email communication**, depending on who Zuhair is (advisor vs senior partner).

However, from a practical advisory standpoint—especially considering how the tax authorities in Pakistan are currently approaching cross-border structures—there are a few critical areas where I would refine, stress, or slightly recalibrate the positioning to make it more defensible in an assessment or audit scenario.

---

## **1. CFC Position under Section 109A – Technically Correct, but Highly Sensitive in Practice**

The advice correctly concludes that Searle FZE can remain outside CFC implications if it qualifies as an **active business company (≥80% income from unrelated parties)**. fileciteturn0file0  

From experience, this is where most structures fail during scrutiny—not because the conclusion is wrong, but because **documentation and substance fall short**.

### Practical risk observation:
- Even if sales are to UAE customers, the tax authorities often question:
  - Whether **pricing is influenced by related party (TSCL)**  
  - Whether FZE is merely a **pass-through entity**

### What I would emphasize further:
- Maintain **clear third-party contracts with UAE customers**
- Ensure **independent decision-making evidence** at FZE level
- Maintain **separate board/management records** (even if same beneficial owner)

👉 In short:  
The conclusion is correct, but **the burden of proof lies entirely on contemporaneous documentation**.

---

## **2. Transfer Pricing – This is the Core Exposure (Not CFC)**

The advice rightly highlights section 108 exposure and recommends documentation. fileciteturn0file0  

However, in real assessments, this becomes the **primary adjustment point**, especially where:
- Pakistan entity is in **minimum tax regime**
- Profits are visibly shifting to a **low-tax jurisdiction (UAE Free Zone)**

### Key practical insight:
FBR officers typically take the position that:
> “If TSCL is manufacturing and assuming core risks, majority profit must remain in Pakistan.”

### What needs stronger emphasis:
- If FZE is **limited-risk**, then:
  - Margin should be **very thin (e.g., 2%–5% range depending on function)**
- If margin is higher:
  - Must demonstrate:
    - Market development role  
    - Regulatory handling  
    - Credit risk assumption  
    - After-sales obligations  

👉 Otherwise, adjustment under section 108 is almost inevitable.

---

## **3. Substance vs Form – This is Where Recharacterization Risk is Real**

The advice correctly flags section 109 recharacterization risk. fileciteturn0file0  

This is **not theoretical**—this is exactly how many audit cases are now being built.

### Based on facts in the advice:
- Direct shipment from Pakistan  
- Back-to-back LCs  
- Minimal inventory risk  

👉 This strongly resembles:
**Commission / agency structure (not buy-sell)**

### Likely FBR stance:
They may argue:
- TSCL is actual seller  
- FZE is only facilitator  
- Therefore:
  - Entire sale belongs to TSCL  
  - Only commission allowed to FZE  

### Practical recommendation (very important):
If current structure continues:
- Either:
  - Strengthen **real distributor substance**, OR  
  - **Shift formally to commission model**  

👉 Because currently:
**Form = Distributor  
Substance = Agent**

And this mismatch is exactly where section 109 is invoked.

---

## **4. Commission Model – In My View, More Defensible**

The advice suggests evaluating a commission model, which I strongly agree with. fileciteturn0file0  

From a Pakistani tax perspective:

### Advantages:
- Eliminates recharacterization risk
- Aligns **legal form with actual conduct**
- Easier transfer pricing benchmarking
- Reduces litigation exposure

### Trade-off:
- TSCL shows **higher revenue in Pakistan**
- But:
  - Cleaner structure  
  - Lower dispute risk  

👉 In practice, many multinationals are moving towards this model for exactly this reason.

---

## **5. Minimum Tax Regime – A Hidden but Important Angle**

The advice briefly mentions that TSCL is under minimum tax regime. fileciteturn0file0  

This is important because:

- Even if profit is shifted out:
  - TSCL still pays minimum tax on turnover  
- BUT:
  - Transfer pricing adjustment can **increase turnover**
  - Leading to:
    - Higher minimum tax  
    - Additional exposure  

👉 So:
This structure **does not eliminate tax risk**, it may only defer or shift it.

## **Overall Professional View (Refined Conclusion)**

The advice is technically robust, but from a **practical risk management perspective**, I would position it as follows:

1. **CFC risk is manageable**  
   → Provided strong documentation and active business test is continuously met  

2. **Transfer pricing is the main exposure**  
   → Margin at FZE must strictly reflect limited functions  

3. **Substance mismatch is the biggest red flag**  
   → Current structure is vulnerable to recharacterization  

4. **Commission model is commercially safer**  
   → Especially given current fact pattern  

---

## **If I Were Advising the Client Directly**

I would recommend:

- Either:
  **(A) Strengthen FZE as real distributor**
  - Warehouse presence  
  - Inventory holding  
  - Commercial risk assumption  
  - Independent operations  

- Or:
  **(B) Shift to commission model (preferred)**
  - Cleaner  
  - Lower audit exposure  
  - More defensible in Pakistan  

---

- Prepare a **risk matrix comparing distributor vs commission model** for decision-making.

# **APPEAL NOTE BEFORE THE APPELLATE TRIBUNAL INLAND REVENUE**  
**Oxford University Press – Pakistan Branch**  
**Tax Periods: 2008 to 2011**

---

## **1. Overview and Core Controversy**

This appeal arises from Order-in-Original dated June 28, 2024 passed under section 14B of the Federal Excise Act, 2005, whereby Federal Excise Duty (FED), along with default surcharge and penalty, has been imposed upon the appellant. fileciteturn0file0  

At its core, the dispute stems from an erroneous assumption by the department that royalty payments made by the appellant to authors constitute “franchise fee” liable to FED. This assumption is factually incorrect and legally unsustainable, as the appellant operates merely as a branch of Oxford University Press (UK), and there exists no franchise arrangement or grant of representational rights. fileciteturn0file1  

However, before even entering into merits, the impugned proceedings fail on **threshold jurisdictional grounds**, particularly **limitation and lack of lawful authority**, which go to the root of the matter.

---

## **2. Chronological Development and How the Matter Became Time-Barred**

A proper appreciation of limitation requires examining the sequence in which events unfolded.

The appellant’s registration itself was a disputed issue from the outset. Although registration was imposed by the department, the same was ultimately set aside through judicial proceedings, culminating in cancellation of STRN on July 9, 2008, based on findings that the appellant was not liable to be registered at all. fileciteturn0file1  

Subsequently, demands were raised through Orders-in-Original during 2010 to 2012, which travelled up to the Tribunal. The learned ATIR, through its order dated July 10, 2013, and more importantly through the **Miscellaneous Application (Rectification) order dated March 18, 2014**, remanded the matter back with a very specific direction — that the **issue of registrability must first be determined in accordance with law**. fileciteturn0file2  

Following this, the department **did initiate remand proceedings pursuant to the MA order**, and notices were issued accordingly. However, these proceedings were **never concluded within the statutory timeframe**.

At this stage, it is critical to understand that the legal life of remand proceedings **commenced from March 18, 2014**, i.e., the date of the MA order, and any proceedings flowing therefrom were required to be completed within the limitation prescribed under section 14B.

Despite initiation, the department allowed the matter to remain dormant and failed to pass any order until June 28, 2024 — nearly a decade later.

During the interregnum, the Honourable Sindh High Court, vide order dated September 14, 2022, disposed of the matter. However, the High Court did **not create any fresh remand jurisdiction**, nor did it revive limitation. The proceedings had already been remanded earlier by the Tribunal, and the department had already exercised that jurisdiction by initiating proceedings — albeit without concluding them.

Therefore, the High Court order cannot be construed as a fresh starting point for limitation. It neither extended time nor authorized re-initiation of proceedings after expiry of statutory period.

In these circumstances, the position becomes clear:

- The **cause of action for remand proceedings originated in 2014**,  
- The department **availed that opportunity but failed to conclude proceedings**, and  
- The statutory timeline expired on **June 30, 2020**, after which no valid order could be passed.

The impugned order dated June 28, 2024 is thus **clearly time-barred**, and any proceedings culminating in such order are void ab initio.

---

## **3. Legal Effect of Time Bar – Not a Procedural Defect but a Jurisdictional Extinction**

It is respectfully submitted that limitation in fiscal statutes is not merely procedural; rather, it extinguishes jurisdiction itself.

Once the statutory time period lapses:

- The authority becomes **functus officio**,  
- The proceedings cannot be revived through administrative action, and  
- Any subsequent order is rendered a nullity in the eyes of law.

In the present case, since the department had already initiated remand proceedings post-2014 but failed to conclude them within limitation, it cannot now rely on subsequent developments (such as High Court order) to **reopen or extend a dead proceeding**.

This is precisely the mischief attempted in the impugned order — i.e., treating the High Court order as a fresh trigger — which is legally impermissible.

---

## **4. Jurisdictional Restriction on Recovery and Continuation of Proceedings**

Even independent of limitation, the department lacked jurisdiction to proceed against the appellant.

The entire scheme of the Federal Excise Act, 2005 applies to **registered persons**, and this position has been specifically acknowledged by the Tribunal itself in earlier proceedings. fileciteturn0file2  

In the present case:

- The appellant’s registration stood cancelled pursuant to judicial findings,  
- Such cancellation had retrospective effect, and  
- The appellant was effectively an **unregistered person since inception**. fileciteturn0file1  

Accordingly, the legal restriction operates in two ways:

First, **proceedings under the FED Act cannot be initiated or continued against an unregistered person**, unless registrability is first lawfully determined.

Second, even if registration were to be assumed, the liability can arise only **prospectively from the date of compulsory registration**, and not for prior periods.

Thus, the department was under a strict legal obligation to first determine registrability — which it failed to do — and in absence thereof, no recovery proceedings could have been lawfully undertaken.

---

## **5. Misplaced Reliance on High Court Order**

The impugned order proceeds on the premise that the Honourable High Court’s order dated September 14, 2022 provided a fresh basis to initiate or conclude remand proceedings.

This interpretation is fundamentally flawed.

The High Court merely disposed of the matter based on existing factual and legal position and did not:

- Remand the matter afresh,  
- Extend limitation, or  
- Authorize re-initiation of proceedings beyond statutory period.

In fact, the only operative remand remains the one issued by ATIR through the MA order dated March 18, 2014, and the department had already acted upon it.

Once that opportunity lapsed due to non-conclusion within limitation, the proceedings could not be revived under the guise of High Court order.

---

## **6. Failure to Determine Registrability – Core Defect in Proceedings**

Even on merits of procedure, the impugned order fails to address the central issue remanded by the Tribunal — i.e., **registrability of the appellant**.

The factual record placed before the department clearly demonstrated that:

- The appellant’s STRN was cancelled following CESTAT decision,  
- The appellant’s activities (publishing and sale of books) were exempt, and  
- Registration was never legally required. fileciteturn0file1  

Despite this, the DCIR bypassed this foundational issue and directly proceeded to levy FED, which is contrary to the explicit directions of the Tribunal and renders the entire exercise legally invalid.

---

## **7. Brief on Merits – Royalty vs Franchise**

Without prejudice to the jurisdictional defects, the levy itself is unsustainable.

The department has treated royalty payments made to authors as “franchise fee”, whereas:

- Authors merely grant publishing rights,  
- No representational rights are involved, and  
- No franchise relationship exists. fileciteturn0file1  

The essential ingredients of franchise — particularly the right to represent the franchisor — are completely absent.

Therefore, even on merits, the demand fails.

---

## **8. Constitutional Limitation – FED on Services**

Another independent restriction arises from the constitutional framework post 18th Amendment.

With effect from July 1, 2011:

- Taxation of services falls within provincial domain, and  
- Federal Excise Duty on services has been held to be unconstitutional. fileciteturn0file2  

Thus, even if the department’s case is accepted arguendo, the levy itself cannot survive on constitutional grounds.

---

## **9. Concluding Position**

In totality, the case presents a clear situation where:

- Proceedings were initiated pursuant to remand in 2014,  
- Not concluded within statutory time (lapsed by June 2020),  
- Wrongly attempted to be revived through misreading of High Court order, and  
- Ultimately culminated in an order passed without jurisdiction in 2024.

Coupled with this are independent defects relating to:

- Non-determination of registrability,  
- Inapplicability of FED to an unregistered person,  
- Incorrect classification of royalty, and  
- Constitutional bar on levy.

---

## **10. Prayer**

In light of the above, it is respectfully prayed that the Honourable Tribunal may be pleased to:

- Declare the impugned order as **time-barred, without jurisdiction and void ab initio**;  
- Delete the entire FED demand along with surcharge and penalty;  
- Direct refund/adjustment of amounts recovered; and  
- Grant any other relief deemed appropriate.

## **5. Jurisdictional Restriction – Proceedings Against Unregistered Person**

Even otherwise, the proceedings are without jurisdiction as the appellant was not a registered person.

The factual record establishes that:

- The appellant’s STRN was cancelled pursuant to judicial findings, and  
- Such cancellation reflects that the appellant was not liable to be registered ab initio. fileciteturn0file1  

The Tribunal itself has held that the provisions of the Federal Excise Act apply only to registered persons and that prior proceedings were invalid for failure to determine registrability. fileciteturn0file2  

Despite this, the department failed to determine registrability and directly proceeded to levy FED, which is contrary to law and binding directions.

---

## **6. Misreading of High Court Order**

The impugned order incorrectly treats the Honourable High Court’s order dated September 14, 2022 as a fresh basis for initiating proceedings.

This interpretation is erroneous because:

- The High Court did not remand the matter afresh,  
- It did not extend limitation, and  
- It did not authorize re-initiation of proceedings.  

The only valid remand remained the Tribunal’s order of March 18, 2014, which had already been acted upon and exhausted.

---

## **7. Brief on Merits – Royalty Is Not Franchise Fee**

Without prejudice to the above jurisdictional defects, the levy itself is unsustainable.

The appellant has consistently demonstrated that:

- Payments are made to authors for publishing rights,  
- No representational rights exist, and  
- No franchise relationship is present. fileciteturn0file1  

Thus, the essential ingredients of franchise are absent, and the classification adopted by the department is legally untenable.

---

## **8. Constitutional Limitation – FED on Services**

An independent bar arises from the constitutional framework post 18th Amendment, whereby taxation of services falls within the provincial domain.

Judicial pronouncements have held that FED on services is unconstitutional post July 1, 2011, and even otherwise, federal authorities cannot assume jurisdiction in respect of such services. fileciteturn0file2  

---

## **9. Conclusion**

The present case clearly demonstrates that:

- Proceedings were initiated pursuant to remand in 2014,  
- Not concluded within statutory limitation (expired in 2020),  
- Wrongly revived on misinterpretation of High Court order, and  
- Ultimately culminated in an order passed without jurisdiction in 2024.  

Coupled with this are independent defects relating to registrability, incorrect classification, and constitutional limitations, all of which render the impugned order unsustainable.

## **10. Prayer**

In light of the above, it is respectfully prayed that the Honourable Tribunal may be pleased to:

- Declare the impugned order as **time-barred, without jurisdiction and void ab initio**;  
- Delete the entire FED demand along with surcharge and penalty;
